results.bodyText: +1 (303) 882-8447npc@drautoimmune.comHomeAbout UsServicesConditionsPatient StoriesBlogShopContact UsBook your Discovery CallBlogAre You Testing Your Inflammatory Markers? Here’s Why You Should Be!November 12, 2025•3 minutesIf you find yourself suffering from anxiety, joint pain, brain fog, thinning hair, or extreme fatigue, and none of your doctors or specialists can diagnose your issues, it is likely time for you to have your inflammatory markers checked.Chronic inflammationis tricky and can lie undetected behind vague symptoms that can get misdiagnosed, and if not treated properly, can result in serious health complications like a heart attack, autoimmune disease, or even dementia. Let’s break it down. Here are six powerful blood tests that could be the missing puzzle piece in your health journey. https://www.tiktok.com/embed/v2/7553776788875349278?lang=en-GB&referrer=https%3A%2F%2Fdrautoimmune.com%2Fblog%2Ftesting-inflammatory-markers%2F 1. High-Sensitivity C-Reactive Protein (hs-CRP) Why it matters:CRPis a protein produced in response to inflammation by your liver. The high sensitivity version (hs-CRP) is 10x more accurate and catches subtle, chronic inflammation much earlier. **Optimal level:**Less than 1.0 If this is elevated, your inflammation is more likely to worsen, placing your tissues at a greater risk of damage. It’s also predictive of future disease risk more than primary autoimmune markers like apositive ANA.2. Ferritin **Why it matters:**Ferritin is known as the body’s storage tank for iron, but it also participates in the differentiation of inflammation from other processes in the body. Target range: Women: 50–150 ng/ml Men: Up to 250 ng/ml If you havehigh ferritin levelsor low ferritin, it might indicate something deeper, like an autoimmune disease or persistent inflammation.3. Homocysteine **Why it matters:**This amino acid positively impacts heart health, brain function (even strokes), along with several cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases. High levels of homocysteine can be problematic because of theMTHFR gene, which determines how you process B vitamins (folate and B12). **Goal:**Under 7 μmol/L If strokes or dementia are in your family history, it is worth it to bring this inflammatory marker up with your doctor if you have never tested it before.4. Fibrinogen Activity **Why it matters:**Fibrinogen is a clotting factor, and high fibrinogen levels can mean there is greater blood viscosity, and the risk of stroke and heart attacks is higher, even in the younger population. The presence of a positive ANA (an autoimmune marker) means there is a greater risk and, therefore, a greater need to control fibrinogen.5. Insulin **Why it matters:**Most people associate insulin with blood sugar; however, it is also a hormonal marker of inflammation. High insulin = hormonal imbalances, leaky gut, and autoimmune activity brewing behind the scenes. If you’re always tired, gaining weight easily, or battling brain fog, insulin could be the culprit. Read More: “Blood Sugar, Dementia & the B12 Connection”6. Vitamin D **Why it matters:**This vitamin does wonders beyond enhancing bone health. Vitamin D also regulates the expression of a number of genes that control inflammation, including a gene called NF-kappa B. Perhaps chronic low levels indicate a deficiency, but then it could also represent a deeper inflammatory struggle your body can’t seem to shake.Inflammatory Markers: The Takeaway If you relentlessly bounce from one provider to another, are told your labs are normal, but feel as though you want to do more, it’s time to dig deeper. These 6 inflammatory markers are better at finding unresolved issues than normal reactors. How about a starting point? We provide telehealth consults focused on identifying root causes and helping you implement a practical, personalized plan. With the right labs, you can find the source of your inflammation, take action, and regain your health. results.bodyText: +1 (303) 882-8447npc@drautoimmune.comHomeAbout UsServicesConditionsPatient StoriesBlogShopContact UsBook your Discovery CallBlogWhat High TSH Levels Actually Mean & Why Thyroid Medication Isn’t Always the AnswerNovember 12, 2025•3 minutesNovember 7, 2025 Has a physician ever told you that you have a “thyroid problem” (aka high TSH levels) and given you a prescription for a thyroid treatment, only for you to feel just as bad or even worse than before? You are not the first, and certainly not the last. Hypothyroidism is one of the most misunderstood conditions in medicine today, and we want to dive into the myths of thyroid hormones, labs, and the reasons why so many people are being misdiagnosed or improperly treated. Time to break it down to you in plain English, no medical degree required. @drautoimmune#tshalterations doesn’t mean#hypothyroidism–#hashimotoscan cause fluctuations and knowing root causes like#insulinresistance#guthealth♬ original sound – drautoimmune High TSH ≠ Hypothyroidism (Every Time) TSH (thyroid stimulating hormone) is commonly the only indicator of thyroid function that most physicians use. If the level is elevated, you’re labeled with hypothyroidism and prescribed a thyroid medication. However, the truth of the matter is: high TSH is not a clear indicator of hypothyroidism. In fact, high TSH levels actually indicate inflammation, usually involving the hypothalamus and pituitary glands, not necessarily just the thyroid. Consider it a waving red flag, not the diagnosis itself. On the other hand, if TSH is elevated and free T4 is decreased, that scenario is more consistent with true hypothyroidism. Read More:Birth Control and Hypothyroidism: What Every Woman Needs to KnowWhy Thyroid Meds Might Make You Feel Worse When individuals start taking thyroid meds, they usually expect to feel better: more energy, less brain fog, etc. But more often, the outcome is feeling like nothing has changed. Worst case? You may feel even worse than before. Don’t ignore it; the real problem is hiding underneath the surface. Traditional medicine’s approach to thyroid health is often missing: Insulin resistance Estrogen dominance Leaky gut syndrome Environmental factors Chronic stress All of these factors can disrupt the connections made in your thyroid. If the body is in a state of chronic inflammation and stress, thyroid hormone treatments won’t help; they’ll just add more fuel to the fire. Read More:Could Iodine Therapy Be Making Your Thyroid Disease Worse?Functional Medicine Labs: Test Smarter, Not Harder Rather than going directly to thyroid meds, take a different approach and look at the bigger picture. As afunctional medicine practitioner, Dr. Ian tests for TSH in addition more inflammatory markers and thyroid hormones, including Free T3 and T4, Reverse T3, and thyroid antibodies. Then, you have a better understanding of what’s causing high TSH levels and can focus on tackling the underlying issues. Address gut health, stabilize hormone balance, minimize toxin exposure, and manage stress. Dr. Autoimmune has helped hundreds of thyroid patients see an improvement in their symptoms, without using prescription medication.Action Plan For Today Stay calm: it’s possible for your thyroid to heal itself when you address the root cause. Ask for help: reach out to us for a more comprehensive view of your health. Dig into your lifestyle: improve your diet, move your body, and prioritize quality sleep. If your current physician is brushing off your concerns, find one who listens. Our online functional medicine telemedicine doctor is ready to hear from you and get to the bottom of your thyroid symptoms.Final Thoughts From Dr. Autoimmune Traditional medicine is sometimes too quick to treat the lab test result rather than looking at the entire person and the bigger picture. Your body is smart and lets you know when something isn’t right. Listen to it and don’t settle for a prescription. Ready to unlock the true cause of your high TSH levels? results.bodyText: +1 (303) 882-8447npc@drautoimmune.comHomeAbout UsServicesConditionsPatient StoriesBlogShopContact UsBook your Discovery CallBlogWhy Your POTS Symptoms Still Don’t Make Sense And What Your Body May Be Trying To Tell YouJune 29, 2026•11 minutesDo you feel dizzy when standing up, exhausted after simple tasks, sensitive to heat, or like your heart races for no obvious reason? Many people experiencing these symptoms have never heard of Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome, commonly known as POTS, while others have already been diagnosed but still do not understand why their body feels so unpredictable. POTS is a form of dysautonomia, which means it involves the autonomic nervous system. This is the part of the body responsible for regulating heart rate, blood pressure, circulation, digestion, temperature control, and stress response without you having to think about it. When this system struggles to regulate properly, symptoms can begin affecting nearly every part of daily life. Many people accept these symptoms as their ‘new normal’ without realizing something deeper may be going on. You may start avoiding hot showers because they make you feel faint. You may stand up and suddenly feel your heart pounding. You may feel completely drained after running errands, shaky after meals, foggy during conversations, or exhausted after doing things that used to feel simple.What POTS Really Feels Like Beyond The Diagnosis POTS is commonly described as a condition involving an abnormal increase in heart rate when moving from lying down to standing. However, most people living with POTS know it rarely feels as simple as a heart rate issue. For many individuals, it feels like the entire body stopped regulating the way it used to. Symptoms can affect energy, circulation, digestion, focus, stress tolerance, and nervous system stability all at once, which is one reason the condition can feel so confusing and overwhelming. Many people with POTS describe: • dizziness when standing • racing heart or heart palpitations • brain fog • fatigue that does not improve with rest • heat intolerance • shakiness after meals • exercise intolerance • shortness of breath • digestive symptoms • nausea or bloating • headaches or migraines • feeling faint in the shower • weakness after simple daily tasks • anxiety sensations without a clear trigger • feeling wired but exhausted • symptoms that flare after stress, illness, heat, poor sleep, or overexertion For many people, life slowly starts revolving around these symptoms. You may begin thinking about where you can sit down, whether the heat will trigger a flare, how much energy you have left for the day, or whether your body is going to cooperate with even the simplest plans. You may cancel outings, avoid exercise, feel anxious before leaving the house, or start questioning whether anyone truly understands what you are dealing with. Over time, that emotional exhaustion can become just as draining as the physical symptoms themselves. Many people are told their labs look normal. Others are told stress or anxiety may be contributing to symptoms. Some are given symptom-management strategies that help temporarily but never seem to create lasting stability. Eventually, many people begin wondering whether there is a deeper explanation beneath the surface. Wondering whether your symptoms may fit common POTS root cause patterns?Download our free POTS Root Cause Assessmentto explore nervous system, immune, gut, circulation, nutrient, and inflammation patterns often missed in conventional care. At Dr. Autoimmune, we provide virtual functional medicine care for patients across the United States, allowing individuals struggling with complex chronic symptoms to receive support from home without the added stress of travel.What Causes POTS? One of the most common questions people ask after receiving a diagnosis is, “What causes POTS?” The answer is not always straightforward. Researchers are still working to better understand why some people develop Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome. While there is rarely a single cause, growing research and clinical observation suggest that several different systems may contribute to the condition. This is one reason POTS symptoms can look very different from person to person and why some individuals respond well to certain approaches while others continue struggling despite doing everything they have been told. Common patterns associated with POTS may include: • viral infections or post-viral syndromes • autoimmune conditions and immune system activation • nervous system dysregulation • iron deficiency or nutrient depletion • hormonal changes • chronic stress and inflammation • connective tissue disorders such as Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome • blood sugar instability • digestive dysfunction and nutrient absorption issues For some individuals, symptoms begin after a significant viral illness such as COVID-19, mononucleosis, or another infection. Others notice symptoms developing after a period of chronic stress, burnout, pregnancy, surgery, or a major life event that placed significant strain on the body. Some research has also explored the connection between POTS and autoimmune activity, suggesting that immune system dysfunction may play a role in certain individuals. Others may struggle with low iron stores, nutrient deficiencies, digestive dysfunction, or nervous system patterns that affect circulation and stress regulation. The important thing to understand is that not everyone with POTS has the same underlying drivers. That is one reason symptoms can vary so dramatically from person to person. It is also one reason many people become frustrated when they are given a one-size-fits-all approach to treatment. At Dr. Autoimmune, we often find that the most important question is not simply whether someone has POTS. The more important question is: What underlying issues have contributed to POTS symptoms developing in the first place? Understanding those deeper patterns is often where the conversation begins to change. While you’re here, check out this great video Dr. Autoimmune did on TikTok.Why Conventional POTS Care Sometimes Feels Incomplete Conventional care for POTS generally focuses on stabilizing heart rate, circulation, and blood volume. Recommendations may include increasing salt and fluids, wearing compression garments, incorporating exercise or physical therapy, and using medications designed to help regulate heart rate and blood pressure. These approaches can absolutely provide symptom relief for some individuals and may improve daily functioning. However, many patients still find themselves asking an important question after trying these strategies for months or even years. Why does my body still feel unstable? At Dr. Autoimmune, we believe that question matters. Symptom management can be helpful, but it does not always explain why symptoms began in the first place or why they continue flaring despite ongoing efforts to manage them. For some individuals, the racing heart may not actually be the root issue. Instead, it may be the body responding to stress, inflammation, immune activity, nutrient depletion, nervous system dysregulation, or post viral changes occurring elsewhere in the system. That distinction is incredibly important because if the heart is reacting to deeper instability, slowing the reaction alone may not fully resolve why the instability developed in the first place.What If The Heart Is Reacting Rather Than Malfunctioning? One of the biggest shifts many people experience when exploring functional medicine is realizing the body may not be randomly malfunctioning. In many cases, symptoms are the body’s response to stress or imbalance happening somewhere deeper beneath the surface. For some people, immune system activity may be influencing nervous system regulation and circulation. Others may have chronic inflammation, low ferritin or iron storage, nutrient depletion, digestive dysfunction, blood sugar instability, post viral changes, or stress hormone dysregulation contributing to symptoms. This does not mean every case of POTS has the same root cause. It means many people may benefit from looking at the body as an interconnected system rather than focusing on one isolated symptom at a time. At Dr. Autoimmune, this is one of the most important perspectives we help patients understand. The body often gives clues long before someone receives a diagnosis. The challenge is that those clues are frequently scattered across multiple systems, making the bigger picture harder to recognize.The Patterns Many People Never Realize Are Connected One of the most common things we hear from patients is that they never realized how many of their symptoms could potentially be connected. Someone may struggle with dizziness and a racing heart, but they may also have digestive issues, chronic fatigue, food sensitivities, anxiety sensations, headaches, heat intolerance, poor stress tolerance, exercise intolerance, or a history of viral illness. Another person may have struggled with low iron, nutrient deficiencies, burnout, sleep disruption, or autoimmune symptoms for years before POTS symptoms became severe enough to disrupt daily life. When symptoms involve multiple systems, many people begin feeling like their body is overreacting to everything. They may feel sensitive to stress, certain foods, temperature changes, exercise, or even normal daily routines. That is often where a root cause approach becomes valuable. Instead of looking at symptoms individually, the focus becomes understanding how immune activity, inflammation, nervous system regulation, digestion, nutrient status, circulation, stress response, and metabolic health may all be interacting together. For many individuals struggling with persistent POTS symptoms, it is not one isolated issue. It is often the overlap between systems that creates the instability. Want to see whether these patterns may apply to you?Download the free POTS Root Cause Assessment.Why Functional Medicine Changes The Entire Conversation Functional medicine changes the strategy because it asks different questions. Instead of only asking how to reduce symptoms, the focus becomes understanding why the symptoms developed and what may still be driving them. At Dr. Autoimmune, we use a structured investigative approach designed for complex chronic conditions. That process often involves looking carefully at a patient’s timeline, symptom progression, immune history, nervous system stress patterns, digestion, inflammation, nutrient status, lifestyle stressors, and possible trigger points that may have contributed to instability over time. This is not about applying generic protocols or assuming every patient has the same root cause. It is about identifying patterns that may have been overlooked in standard care and building a more personalized strategy based on those findings. Dr. Ian Hollaman, DC, MSc, FMCP, also known as Dr. Autoimmune, has more than 17 years of experience working with chronic, unresolved health conditions. His work focuses on helping people better understand the underlying contributors to symptoms involving dizziness, fatigue, nervous system dysregulation, post viral syndromes, immune imbalance, circulation issues, digestive dysfunction, and chronic inflammation. For many patients, simply having someone step back and look at the full picture can feel incredibly validating after years of fragmented care and unanswered questions.Why So Many People Feel Emotionally Exhausted By POTS One of the most overlooked parts of living with POTS is the emotional exhaustion that develops over time. When your body feels unpredictable, it can slowly affect every area of life. Work becomes harder. Relationships become harder. Social activities feel harder. You may begin avoiding situations because you are worried about flaring, crashing, or feeling embarrassed by symptoms you cannot control. Some people begin grieving the version of themselves they used to be before symptoms disrupted their energy, confidence, and sense of normalcy. Others become exhausted from constantly searching for answers while trying to hold life together at the same time. That emotional burden matters. At Dr. Autoimmune, we believe people deserve more than being told to simply manage symptoms forever without understanding what may actually be driving the instability underneath them. Even when symptoms are complex, understanding the deeper patterns involved can completely change how someone views their body and their path forward. When symptoms stop looking random, people often stop blaming themselves. And for many individuals, that shift alone becomes incredibly powerful.How The POTS Root Cause Assessment Can Help The POTS Root Cause Assessment was designed to help individuals begin identifying patterns that may be contributing to their symptoms. It is not a diagnosis and it is not meant to replace medical care. Instead, it is a structured pattern recognition tool designed to help people look at their symptoms through a broader functional medicine lens. Inside the assessment, individuals walk through patterns involving nervous system stress, immune and post viral changes, digestive and inflammatory symptoms, circulation patterns, and iron or nutrient-related issues that are commonly seen in chronic complex cases. For many people, this becomes the first time they begin recognizing how many of their symptoms may actually be connected. That awareness can be incredibly important because once the pattern becomes clearer, the next steps often become clearer as well.You Deserve More Than Temporary Symptom Management If you have been struggling with POTS symptoms that still do not fully make sense, you are not alone. Many people spend years trying to manage symptoms without ever feeling like they truly understand what changed in their body. At Dr. Autoimmune, we believe you deserve more than temporary fixes that only address the surface-level reaction. You deserve to explore whether deeper patterns involving the nervous system, immune system, inflammation, digestion, circulation, nutrient status, or post viral changes may be contributing to your symptoms. Our goal is to help patients move beyond confusion and begin understanding the bigger picture behind what their body may be trying to communicate. Start with thePOTS Root Cause Assessment to begin connecting the dots. If you feel like your symptoms still do not fully make sense, Dr. Ian Hollaman and his team may be able to help you explore whether a deeper functional medicine approach is appropriate for your situation. If you’ve tried conventional strategies and still feel like something is missing, a Discovery Call can help you explore whether a root cause functional medicine approach may be the right next step. Click here to book your Discovery calltoday. You deserve more than constantly trying to “push through” symptoms that continue disrupting your energy, confidence, and quality of life. results.bodyText: +1 (303) 882-8447npc@drautoimmune.comHomeAbout UsServicesConditionsPatient StoriesBlogShopContact UsBook your Discovery CallBlogLeaky Gut Care: Find a Specialist in BoulderMay 10, 2026•7 minutesHow Healing Your Gut Can Transform Autoimmune Health Leaky gut is a simple phrase for something quite technical, increased intestinal permeability. Your gut lining is meant to act like a smart filter, letting in nutrients while keeping out larger particles, toxins, and microbes. When that lining becomes irritated and less selective, more things pass into the bloodstream and the immune system can react. For people living with autoimmune or stubborn chronic symptoms, that irritated barrier can be one hidden piece of the puzzle. Spring is a natural time to pay attention to this. Diets shift, we grill more, travel more, and many people notice changes in digestion, allergies and energy. Supporting gut health during this season can help calm immune reactivity as we head into warmer weather. At Dr. Autoimmune, we work through a functional and integrative lens, offering 100% remote support so you can work with a leaky gut specialist in Boulder even if you live elsewhere in Colorado or beyond. Our goal is to explain what leaky gut really is, connect it to symptoms many people think are just “how their body is”, and share the root-cause strategies we use every day.What Leaky Gut Really Is and Why It Happens Your gut lining is only one cell thick, but it does a powerful job. Those cells sit side by side with “tight junctions” that open and close in a controlled way. When this system works well, it allows digested nutrients to move through while keeping bigger or harmful particles inside the gut to be removed. Under ongoing stress, those tight junctions can loosen, and the barrier becomes more “leaky”. Common triggers that can stress the gut lining include: Diets heavy in ultra-processed foods Gluten sensitivity or other food reactions Environmental toxins and chemicals Frequent use of some medications like NSAIDs Ongoing stress and poor sleep Regular alcohol intake Gut infections or microbiome imbalances In functional medicine, we often use the term leaky gut because it is easier to understand, while in conventional gastroenterology you might hear “increased intestinal permeability”. These are related ideas, simply viewed through different lenses. Both are interested in the barrier of the gut, the immune system that sits behind it, and how that affects the whole body. It is also important to remember that not everyone exposed to these triggers develops clear problems. Genetics, immune resilience, childhood health, current lifestyle and even how someone manages stress all play a part. Two people may eat the same diet, but one might develop gut symptoms and autoimmunity while the other feels fine. This is why we always look at the full picture, not just one test or one trigger.Silent Signs Your Gut Barrier May Be Struggling Leaky gut does not always show up as dramatic digestive pain. It often looks like a mix of small, nagging issues that feel easy to dismiss. On the digestive side, we often hear about: Bloating or fullness after even simple meals Constipation, loose stools or flipping between the two Heartburn or reflux New or growing food intolerances These can flare when routines change. More barbecues, eating on the road, and rich restaurant meals in spring and summer can put extra strain on a gut that is already sensitive. Then there are the non-digestive clues, which can be just as telling: Brain fog or trouble focusing Ongoing fatigue that sleep does not fully fix Joint pain or aches without clear injury Skin problems like eczema, psoriasis or acne Sinus congestion and seasonal allergies Mood shifts, anxiety or feeling “on edge” The gut and immune system are tightly linked. A large part of the immune system sits just behind the gut lining. When that barrier is irritated, the immune system can become more reactive, which can play a role in conditions like Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, coeliac disease and chronic fatigue. This does not mean leaky gut is the only cause, but it is often one important piece. We always caution people not to self-diagnose from checklists online. These patterns are signals, not a final answer. If you see yourself in several of these areas, it is a sign that a deeper, professional look at your gut and immune health could be helpful.How a Functional Medicine Doctor Tests and Treats Leaky Gut When someone works with a leaky gut specialist in Boulder through our remote clinic, we start with a careful story. We want to know how symptoms began, what makes them worse or better, and how digestion, hormones, stress, sleep and life events fit together. That history guides which tests and which steps make sense. Assessment may include: Detailed stool analysis to look at microbes, digestion and inflammation Markers related to intestinal permeability Food immune reactivity testing where appropriate From there, we usually move through a root-cause approach that can be thought of in three broad steps: **Remove:**We work to identify and reduce triggers. That may include certain foods, ongoing infections, toxin exposure or, with your prescribing team, a review of frequent medications that might affect the gut. Replace and Rebalance: Some people need support for stomach acid, bile flow or digestive enzymes. Others need specific strategies to calm or shift an imbalanced microbiome. **Repair:**We use targeted nutrients and botanicals aimed at soothing the gut lining and calming irritation, always tailored to the person’s health history and current medications. No two plans look the same. Someone with coeliac disease needs a very different plan from someone with SIBO or strong histamine reactions. Timing, food plans and supplement choices all change based on your unique picture. Because our care is fully remote, people inside and outside the Boulder area can access this kind of in-depth support through video visits and secure online tools.Everyday Habits to Support a Resilient Gut Lining While testing and guided treatment matter, daily habits are the base. Seasonal shifts can make it easier to build gut-friendly routines, because fresh foods and outdoor time are often more available. On the nutrition side, many people do well when they: Focus on fresh, whole, minimally processed foods Include a variety of fibre-rich vegetables and fruits Add healthy fats like olive oil and omega-3-rich foods Include fermented foods if tolerated Stay well hydrated, especially as days get warmer Lifestyle habits matter too. Gentle stress support practices such as simple breathwork, light yoga or quiet walks outside can help calm the stress signals that affect the gut. Prioritising regular sleep, even when evenings are lighter, gives the gut time to repair. Moderate movement, not extreme overtraining, tends to be kinder to both digestion and immunity. It can also help to be thoughtful with alcohol and caffeine, as both can irritate the gut lining for some people. Summer often brings more restaurant meals, travel days and festival-style food. Simple planning can reduce the impact: Keep easy, gut-friendly snacks on hand while travelling Choose grilled, baked or steamed options more often than fried Ask for sauces or dressings on the side if you are sensitive Balance richer meals with lighter, home-cooked options the next day Supplements like glutamine, zinc carnosine or certain probiotics are often mentioned in relation to gut repair. These can be powerful tools, but they are not right for everyone, especially if you have autoimmunity or take several medications. We strongly suggest choosing and dosing these with professional guidance.Take the Next Step Toward Gut-Centred Healing If you recognise yourself in the symptoms and patterns we have described, it may be time to look more closely at your gut barrier and immune health. At Dr. Autoimmune, we are a functional and integrative medicine practice focused on root causes, working 100% remotely so people who want support from a leaky gut specialist in Boulder can do so from the comfort of home. Many people feel relief simply knowing there is a logical way to connect their scattered symptoms. A structured evaluation usually includes a detailed intake, thoughtful lab choices and a plan that blends nutrition, lifestyle shifts and targeted therapeutic support. Addressing gut health now can support your immunity, energy and resilience for the seasons ahead, rather than waiting for symptoms to build.Take The Next Step Toward Healing Your Gut If you are ready to address the root cause of your symptoms with a personalised approach, we invite you to speak with a leaky gut specialist in Boulder at Dr. Autoimmune. In a complimentary discovery call, we will listen to your story, review your concerns and outline practical next steps tailored to you. results.bodyText: +1 (303) 882-8447npc@drautoimmune.comHomeAbout UsServicesConditionsPatient StoriesBlogShopContact UsBook your Discovery CallBlogUnderstanding Gluten Disorders: Celiac Disease, Allergy, and SensitivityFebruary 12, 2026•3 minutesGluten is a protein found in wheat, barley, rye, and related grains. It is a common ingredient in many foods, including bread, pasta, and cereal. While gluten is safe for most people to consume, it can cause health problems for those with gluten-related disorders. In this article, we will explore the differences between celiac disease, gluten allergy, and gluten sensitivity. Celiac Disease Celiac disease is an autoimmune disorder that affects about 1% of the population. It is caused by an immune reaction to gluten, which damages the small intestine. This damage can lead to malabsorption of nutrients and a range of health problems, including anemia, osteoporosis, and neurological disorders. The symptoms of celiac disease can vary widely and may include abdominal pain, bloating, diarrhea, constipation, fatigue, and weight loss. Some people with celiac disease may not have any symptoms at all. The only way to diagnose celiac disease is through a blood test and biopsy of the small intestine. The treatment for celiac disease is a strict gluten-free diet. This means avoiding all foods that contain gluten, including wheat, barley, rye, and related grains. It is important for people with celiac disease to read food labels carefully and avoid cross-contamination with gluten-containing foods. Gluten Allergy A gluten allergy is a type of food allergy that affects a small percentage of the population. Unlike celiac disease, which is an autoimmune disorder, a gluten allergy is an immune system reaction to the proteins in gluten. The symptoms of a gluten allergy can range from mild to severe and may include hives, itching, swelling, nausea, vomiting, and difficulty breathing. In rare cases, a gluten allergy can cause anaphylaxis, which is a life-threatening allergic reaction. The treatment for a gluten allergy is to avoid all foods that contain gluten. People with a gluten allergy should carry an epinephrine auto-injector with them at all times in case of anaphylaxis. Gluten Sensitivity Gluten sensitivity, also known as non-celiac gluten sensitivity, is a condition in which a person experiences symptoms similar to those of celiac disease or a gluten allergy, but does not have an autoimmune or allergic reaction to gluten. The symptoms of gluten sensitivity can include abdominal pain, bloating, diarrhea, constipation, headache, fatigue, and joint pain. The symptoms can be similar to those of celiac disease or a gluten allergy, but they are generally less severe. The diagnosis of gluten sensitivity is based on symptoms and the exclusion of celiac disease and gluten allergy. There is currently no specific test for gluten sensitivity. The treatment for gluten sensitivity is to avoid gluten-containing foods. The Bottom Line Gluten-related disorders can cause a range of health problems, from mild discomfort to life-threatening reactions. Celiac disease is an autoimmune disorder that affects about 1% of the population. It is caused by an immune reaction to gluten, which damages the small intestine. The only treatment for celiac disease is a strict gluten-free diet. A gluten allergy is a type of food allergy that affects a small percentage of the population. The symptoms of a gluten allergy can range from mild to severe and can include hives, itching, swelling, and difficulty breathing. The treatment for a gluten allergy is to avoid all foods that contain gluten. Gluten sensitivity, also known as non-celiac gluten sensitivity, is a condition in which a person experiences symptoms similar to those of celiac disease or a gluten allergy but does not have an autoimmune or allergic reaction to gluten. The diagnosis of gluten sensitivity is based on symptoms, and the treatment is to avoid gluten-containing foods. results.bodyText: +1 (303) 882-8447npc@drautoimmune.comHomeAbout UsServicesConditionsPatient StoriesBlogShopContact UsBook your Discovery CallBlogNutritional Deficiencies in Hashimoto's: Understanding, Prevention, & SupportFebruary 12, 2026•4 minutesHashimoto’s Thyroiditis, also known as Hashimoto’s disease, is an autoimmune condition that affects the thyroid gland. It is characterized by chronic inflammation of the thyroid, which can lead to an underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism). In this blog, we will explore what Hashimoto’s is, who it affects the most, and its prevalence among different age groups. We’ll also delve into common nutritional deficiencies in Hashimoto’s, essential vitamins, the connection to low vitamin D, the importance of zinc, nutrients that support Hashimoto’s, the role of diet, and how functional medicine can be a valuable approach for managing this condition.What is Hashimoto’s Thyroiditis? Hashimoto’s Thyroiditis is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system mistakenly attacks the thyroid gland, causing inflammation and damage. This leads to a gradual decline in thyroid function and a range of symptoms, including fatigue, weight gain, and cold intolerance. It primarily affects women, with a female-to-male ratio of around 10:1. While Hashimoto’s can occur at any age, it’s most commonly diagnosed between the ages of 30 and 60.Common Nutritional Deficiencies in Hashimoto’s Iodine: Iodine is essential for thyroid hormone production. A deficiency can worsen thyroid dysfunction in Hashimoto’s. Selenium: Selenium helps reduce inflammation and protect the thyroid from autoimmune attacks. Iron: Anemia due to iron deficiency can exacerbate fatigue, a common symptom in Hashimoto’s. **Vitamin B12:**Low B12 levels can contribute to fatigue and nerve damage, which can be mistaken for Hashimoto’s symptoms. Magnesium: Magnesium supports enzyme reactions involved in thyroid hormone production and immune regulation. Vitamin D: Autoimmune diseases like Hashimoto’s can lead to chronic inflammation, which can affect the body’s ability to utilize vitamin D, which is why a vitamin D deficiency is so common. Additionally, individuals with Hashimoto’s often avoid direct sun exposure, which is a natural source of vitamin D, due to photosensitivity.The Most Important Vitamins and Minerals for Hashimoto’s Vitamin D: Adequate vitamin D levels are crucial for immune regulation and can help reduce the risk of autoimmune thyroid diseases. A great supplement for Vitamin D repletion is Dr. Autoimmune’s D3 Power. It not only helps replete Vitamin D but also helps with joint & muscle support and immune system support. Vitamin A: Supports thyroid hormone synthesis and immune function. Vitamin E: An antioxidant that helps reduce inflammation and oxidative stress. Zinc:Zinc is vital for thyroid hormone production and immune system function. It can help modulate the immune response in Hashimoto’s and reduce inflammation. Zinc deficiency can worsen thyroid function and increase the risk of autoimmune attacks. Selenium:Selenium is essential for reducing inflammation and protecting the thyroid from autoimmune attacks.Nutrients That Help Prevent and Support Hashimoto’s Omega-3 Fatty Acids: Found in fish and flaxseed, these can help reduce inflammation. Probiotics: A healthy gut microbiome is crucial for immune system balance. L-carnitine: Supports energy production and reduces fatigue. Zinc: Zinc is essential for thyroid hormone production and immune function, it can help modulate the immune response and reduce inflammation. Dr. Autoimmune’s Min Power supplement is packed full of zinc/selenium which makes it a great choice for prevention and support. Immunity Support Supplements: Any supplements that enhance the immune system like Dr. Autoimmune’s Immuno Power can help prevent and support Hashimoto’s. Also supplements such as vitamin C can provide additional support.How Diet Affects Hashimoto’s Disease A well-balanced diet that includes foods rich in the nutrients mentioned above can help manage Hashimoto’s. Additionally, some people find relief from symptoms by eliminating gluten, as it can exacerbate inflammation and autoimmunity in some cases. A diet high in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains can provide essential nutrients and fiber to support overall health.Functional Medicine and Dr. Autoimmune Functional medicine offers a holistic approach to managing Hashimoto’s Thyroiditis. It focuses on addressing the root causes of the disease rather than just alleviating symptoms. This approach involves personalized dietary recommendations, targeted supplementation, lifestyle modifications, and stress management. Functional medicine practitioners aim to optimize the patient’s health, taking into account individual circumstances and genetic factors. When seeking expert guidance in managing Hashimoto’s, Dr. Ian Hollaman DC, MSc, IFMCP aka Dr. Autoimmune stands as a forerunner in autoimmune and functional medicine care. The uniqueness of Dr. Autoimmune’s program lies in its accessibility – it is 100% remote, making it available to individuals worldwide. By embracing innovative approaches to Hashimoto’s management, individuals can receive personalized care and support, ultimately helping them lead healthier lives while managing this autoimmune condition. In conclusion, Hashimoto’s Thyroiditis is a complex autoimmune condition that requires a multifaceted approach to management. Understanding common nutritional deficiencies, essential vitamins, minerals, and the importance of a well-balanced diet is crucial. Functional medicine, coupled with Dr. Autoimmune’s remote program offers a promising path for individuals seeking comprehensive care and support in their journey to manage Hashimoto’s. results.bodyText: +1 (303) 882-8447npc@drautoimmune.comHomeAbout UsServicesConditionsPatient StoriesBlogShopContact UsBook your Discovery CallBlogFirst Autoimmune Functional Medicine Visit GuideMay 3, 2026•7 minutesYour first functional medicine visit for autoimmune disease can feel like a big step. You may wonder what will happen, which tests will be ordered, how long it will all take, and what it might cost over time. When you know what to expect, it is easier to feel calm, ask clear questions, and make steady progress. In this article, we will walk through how functional medicine looks at autoimmunity, what happens during a first remote visit, common testing, timelines, general cost categories, and how to prepare. Our team at Dr. Autoimmune offers 100 percent remote care, so whether you are seeking a functional medicine consultation in Boulder or live many states away, you can get started from home. Spring can be a natural time to reset, and early May is often when people feel ready for a fresh start.How Functional Medicine Approaches Autoimmune Disease Functional medicine looks at autoimmune disease in a different way than many conventional models. Instead of focusing only on symptom control, we look for what may be driving the immune system out of balance. We look at your whole story and how different parts of your body affect each other. In practice, that means we often evaluate multiple “root-cause” areas at once, because they can interact and contribute to immune dysfunction. Areas we often think about include: Gut health and digestion Hormone balance and thyroid function Environmental toxins and infections Stress load, mood, and sleep quality Nutrition, blood sugar, and movement Personalized care is more than changing a few foods or adding a standard supplement list. We aim to build care around your symptoms, history, priorities, and capacity, which often includes a careful history, targeted testing, and a plan that is realistic for your day-to-day life. Personalized care can include: A detailed health and symptom history Labs that match your specific condition and goals A plan that fits your life, not a one-size-fits-all plan With autoimmune disease, the long-term goal is usually to calm or slow the process, reduce the frequency and intensity of flares, and support a better quality of life. It is not realistic to expect an overnight cure, but many people can work toward fewer bad days and more stable days over time.What to Expect at Your First Virtual Visit At Dr. Autoimmune, the first visit happens fully online through a secure video call. Before we meet, you complete intake forms so we can start to see patterns in your health story. During the first visit, we use your intake as a starting point and then build a fuller picture together through questions and discussion. A typical first visit often includes: Review of your intake forms and main concerns In-depth conversation about symptoms and history Discussion of possible root causes to explore An initial, simple plan to start right away To understand your autoimmune pattern and what might be contributing to it, we may ask detailed questions across several systems and life phases. We may ask about: When your symptoms started and how they have changed Digestion, bowel habits, bloating, and heartburn Energy, brain fog, and sleep patterns Menstrual history, pregnancy history, and thyroid history when relevant Family history of autoimmunity or other chronic illness Past infections, travel, mold exposure, or toxin exposure Prior lab work, imaging, and diagnoses Because there is a lot to cover, we help you focus on clear, short-term goals for the next 60 to 90 days. For example, we might aim for steadier energy, fewer flares, or better sleep as we work through spring and into summer. Bigger goals, like deeper immune balance, often take more time and extra visits.Common Tests Ordered and How the Process Works Testing choices are based on your symptoms, history, goals, and budget. Many people start with foundational blood work that helps us see the bigger picture of your health and identify patterns that can guide next steps. Common starting labs can include: Complete blood count and comprehensive metabolic panel Thyroid panel, often including thyroid antibodies Inflammatory markers Nutrient status, such as iron markers, vitamin D, B12, folate, and magnesium Blood sugar and insulin markers Cholesterol and other lipid markers Depending on your case, we may also discuss specialty or functional tests. These are typically chosen when they match the clinical picture or when foundational labs and history suggest we need a deeper look at digestion, immune triggers, hormones, or exposures. Options may include: Comprehensive stool testing for gut health, infections, and digestion Food sensitivity or food reaction testing SIBO breath testing when small intestine issues are suspected Hormone and adrenal pattern testing Toxin or heavy metal testing Expanded autoantibody panels when needed From there, the process usually follows a predictable rhythm, even though exact timing varies by lab and test type. Here is how the timeline often looks: After the visit, blood work is usually drawn locally, and home test kits are shipped to you when needed. Many test results return within about 2 to 4 weeks, though some can take longer. We then review results with you during a follow-up visit, fold them into your plan, and decide on next steps. This is part of a multi-visit care plan. The first visit sets the direction, lab results add more detail, and follow-ups help shape and adjust your plan over time.Timelines, Investment, and Insurance Basics Healing with autoimmune disease usually happens over months and seasons, not days. Many people move through phases, and it can help to know that improvement often comes in layers rather than all at once. Many people move through phases like: Early symptom relief and better daily rhythms Stabilization with fewer big ups and downs Deeper repair work and long-term maintenance It is common to need several visits, testing, and ongoing plan updates. Progress is not always a straight line. Some people feel changes early, while others see slow but steady shifts. From a cost point of view, there are a few main buckets to think about. These categories can help you plan ahead and decide how to pace your care based on priorities and budget. Initial visit fee and follow-up visits over time Lab testing, from basic blood work to any specialty tests you choose Supplements or targeted nutrients suggested for your case Nutrition or health coaching support when this is part of your plan Insurance coverage for functional medicine can vary. Some lab tests may be partly covered, while others may not be. Many people use HSA or FSA funds for parts of their care. We encourage you to think of this work as an investment in root-cause care that may help reduce future crises, time away from work, and long stretches of feeling unwell.How to Prepare so You Get the Most From Your Visit Good preparation can make your first visit smoother and more helpful. A little organization ahead of time can help us spend more of your appointment connecting the dots instead of tracking down details. In the weeks before your appointment, it can help to: Complete intake forms with as much detail as you can Keep a 3- to 7-day log of food, symptoms, bowel habits, and energy Collect past lab results and medical records that relate to your condition It is also useful to spend some time in quiet reflection so you can communicate what matters most to you and what constraints we need to respect. You might write down: Your top 3 health goals for the next 3, 6, and 12 months The main stressors in your life right now Non-negotiables, such as work hours or family duties that may shape your plan On the day of your virtual visit, a few practical steps can reduce stress and help the visit run smoothly. Try to: Choose a quiet, private space with a steady internet connection Test your video and audio a few minutes ahead of time Have your logs, records, and a list of questions nearby Be ready to talk honestly about possible lab orders, timelines, and your budget comfort zone This kind of clear, open start helps us create a plan that is medically thoughtful and also realistic for your life.Taking Your Next Step Toward Calmer Autoimmunity You do not have to wait for your next major flare to seek support. Starting a functional medicine plan in the spring can be a helpful time to focus on routines, build resilience, and prepare your body and mind for the seasons ahead. When you come to Dr. Autoimmune for a remote functional medicine consultation in Boulder or from another location, you can expect a thorough first conversation, thoughtful testing options, a step-by-step timeline, clear explanations about general cost categories, and a collaborative plan tailored to your autoimmune picture. Our goal is to help you feel informed, involved, and ready to play an active role in your own care.Reclaim Your Health With Personalized Functional Care If you are ready to address the root causes of your symptoms instead of just managing them, we invite you to schedule a functional medicine consultation in Boulder. At Dr. Autoimmune, we take the time to understand your history, your lifestyle, and your goals so we can create a tailored plan that supports lasting change. results.bodyText: +1 (303) 882-8447npc@drautoimmune.comHomeAbout UsServicesConditionsPatient StoriesBlogShopContact UsBook your Discovery CallBlogWhy Mold Illness Often Mimics Autoimmune Disease SymptomsApril 6, 2026•6 minutesFeeling like your body is attacking you, but every test is “normal” or unclear can be very confusing. Many people live for years with fatigue, pain, brain fog, gut issues, and strange rashes, being told they “probably” have an autoimmune condition, yet nothing quite fits. One missing piece that often surprises people is mold illness. When the immune system reacts to mold and its toxins, the symptoms can look a lot like autoimmunity. In this article, we will talk about how mold illness can mimic autoimmune disease, the clues that mold may be driving your flares, and how a root-cause functional approach can help untangle what is really going on. This is especially important in places with snow, spring rains, and older homes, like around Boulder, where hidden moisture problems are very common.When “Autoimmune” Symptoms Are Not Autoimmune at All Many people go from doctor to doctor with a long list of symptoms, like: Crushing fatigue Achy joints and muscles Brain fog and poor focus Rashes or odd skin changes Bloating, constipation, or loose stools They are told: “It sounds autoimmune.” Medications may be tried, sometimes with little improvement. Over time, it can feel like no one is seeing the full picture. Mold illness can hide under this “mystery autoimmune” label. The problem is that mold and its toxins can trigger inflammation all through the body, so the symptoms overlap heavily with many autoimmune conditions. In communities like Boulder, snowmelt, spring rain, older basements, and roof issues can lead to slow, hidden water damage. A small leak behind a wall or in a crawlspace may go unnoticed for years, while the body quietly reacts to the mold that grows there.How Mold Illness Hijacks the Immune System When we talk about mold illness in this context, we are not just talking about a regular mold allergy. A simple allergy is usually an IgE response that causes sneezing, watery eyes, and quick reactions. Mold illness and other biotoxin illnesses are different. Here is what we often see: Certain indoor molds release toxins called mycotoxins into the air and dust Some people are more sensitive to these toxins than others Their innate immune system, the first line of defense, stays switched “on” This constant activation can drive whole-body inflammation This state can look a lot like autoimmune activation. The immune system is over-alert, sending out inflammatory signals called cytokines. Lab work may show abnormal inflammatory markers. Sometimes there are even low-level autoantibodies that confuse the picture. From the outside, it can seem like an autoimmune disease, but the original trigger is an ongoing exposure to a moldy environment, not an immune system that randomly turned on itself.Symptom Overlap Between Mold Illness and Autoimmune Disease Mold illness and autoimmune conditions share many of the same symptoms. This is one reason mold-related problems are often missed. Shared whole-body symptoms often include: Deep, unrefreshing fatigue Muscle and joint pain Headaches or pressure in the head Brain fog, poor memory, and word-finding issues Mood changes like anxiety or low mood Poor sleep and trouble staying asleep Feeling too hot or too cold We also see overlap in specific organs: **Gut:**bloating, gas, constipation, loose stools, IBS-type issues, SIBO patterns, and leaky gut features Skin: rashes, hives, red or itchy patches that look like eczema or psoriasis **Lungs and sinuses:**chronic cough, stuffy nose, recurrent sinus symptoms, or asthma-like tightness One red flag for mold illness is when symptoms are: Fluctuating or coming and going without clear reason Migrating around the body, like pain that moves from joint to joint Worse in some buildings than others If your “autoimmune” flares get worse at home, in the office, or during wetter seasons, that pattern deserves a closer look at.Clues Mold May Be Driving Your “Autoimmune” Flares While only a full evaluation can sort this out, there are some common clues that mold might be playing a major role. Environmental clues: Visible mold growth, even small spots around windows, in showers, or on basement walls Musty, earthy, or “old basement” smells Water stains on ceilings or walls History of roof leaks, plumbing leaks, ice dams, or basement seepage after snow or spring rain Personal health clues: Symptoms that improve when you travel or spend a long weekend away Feeling worse in a certain room, like a basement office or bedroom Flares that spike during damp weather or right after a leak A long history of confusing diagnoses, with treatments that only help a little or not at all Family or household clues: Other people in the same home struggling with similar unexplained issues Pets with odd skin, breathing, or energy problems When several of these clues line up, it can suggest a shared environmental trigger rather than separate, unrelated illnesses.How a Mold-Savvy Functional Doctor Evaluates You A functional and integrative approach does not just look at one symptom or one lab result. It looks for patterns over time. A thoughtful evaluation often includes: A detailed health history, from childhood to now A full timeline of when symptoms began, and what was happening in your life at that time Questions about every place you have lived or worked, including leaks, damp basements, or musty areas Discussion of past infections, gut issues, and stressors Testing strategies may include: Targeted blood work to look at inflammation, immune markers, nutrient status, and to rule in or out certain autoimmune conditions Specialized mold and mycotoxin testing when the history points to mold exposure Careful review of autoimmune markers, not just a quick “positive” or “negative” label Because many people feel too sick to travel or leave a possibly moldy space for long, remote care can be very helpful. A mold illness doctor in Boulder who works fully online can support people locally and beyond without adding more stress.Natural Treatment Strategies That Calm an Overloaded Immune System Support for mold-related illness focuses on calming the immune system and lowering the total load on the body. This is not about quick fixes, but steady, thoughtful steps. Foundational steps often include: Identifying and reducing exposure to mold, sometimes with home assessment and professional remediation Using air filtration to lower the amount of particles you breathe Simplifying personal care and cleaning products to reduce other toxins in your space Gentle detox and support can involve: Targeted binders that are used under guidance Nutrients that support the liver and lymph system Antioxidants and mitochondrial support, to help with energy and recovery Herbal or, when needed, pharmaceutical antifungals, used thoughtfully and not as a first or only step Because mold and autoimmunity both stress the gut and immune system, we often focus on repair: Anti-inflammatory eating patterns, tailored to your needs and sensitivities Gut healing protocols to support the microbiome and gut lining Nervous system support, like breathwork, pacing, and other strategies that help the body shift out of constant “alarm mode” When exposure is lowered and the body is supported, the immune system often becomes less reactive, and symptoms that looked autoimmune may settle down.Finding the Right Mold Illness Partner in Boulder and Beyond Sorting out mold illness from true autoimmune disease is complex, and many people have some degree of both. This is why it helps to work with someone who understands autoimmune patterns, environmental triggers, and the immune system as a whole, instead of treating each symptom in isolation. At Dr. Autoimmune, we focus on root-cause, functional and integrative care for people with complex, chronic symptoms. For those searching for a mold illness doctor in Boulder or from other locations, our fully remote model makes it possible to get expert guidance while staying in the place that currently feels safest for your body.Take The Next Step Toward Healing From Mold Illness If you are ready to get to the root of your symptoms and feel like yourself again, schedule a discovery call with our mold illness doctor in Boulder. At Dr. Autoimmune, we take the time to listen, understand your history, and build a plan tailored to your needs. You can also contact us with questions about our approach or to learn what to expect at your first visit. results.bodyText: +1 (303) 882-8447npc@drautoimmune.comHomeAbout UsServicesConditionsPatient StoriesBlogShopContact UsBook your Discovery CallBlogCould a Functional Medicine Doctor Help Reverse Autoimmune Flares?April 26, 2026•6 minutesSpring can feel tricky when you live with an autoimmune condition. As the days get longer around Boulder, pollen rises, weather changes from warm to a snowy in a day, and routines shift. For many people, that means more joint pain, fatigue, rashes, or brain fog right when they want to be outside more. It can feel like your body is working against the season. In our functional and integrative medicine practice, we focus on finding what is driving those flares and helping calm the immune system from the inside out. We may not be able to erase an autoimmune diagnosis, but we often see that when triggers are addressed and the whole body is supported, flares slow down, remission stretches longer, and life starts to feel bigger again. Let us walk through how a functional medicine doctor can support that process.How Functional Medicine Helps Calm Spring Autoimmune Flares In Boulder, spring often brings: Tree and grass pollen that aggravate allergies Fast shifts between dry, cold days and warm, windy ones A quick jump in outdoor workouts, hikes, and social events Changes in sleep and eating patterns as daylight shifts All of these can stress an already sensitive immune system. A functional medicine doctor looks at this differently than standard symptom-based care. Instead of only asking, “How do we quiet this flare right now?”, we ask what is irritating the immune system in the first place, how gut health, nutrient status, and stress load are setting the stage for flares, and which pieces of your daily life are pushing your body over its threshold. We focus on root causes and on how all your systems talk to each other. While we cannot promise to “cure” autoimmunity, many people can cool inflammation, feel fewer symptoms, and experience what feels like a reversal of flare-ups through steady, personalized changes.Why Autoimmune Symptoms Flare in the First Place An autoimmune flare is a period when the immune system goes into overdrive. The body starts reacting to its own tissues more strongly, which can show up as: More pain or stiffness Gut issues, like bloating or loose stools Skin changes, such as rashes or hives Brain fog, headaches, and heavier fatigue Many different factors can spark or worsen that overactivity. Common triggers include: Seasonal allergies and pollen exposure Viral or bacterial infections Food sensitivities or inflammatory foods Ongoing stress and emotional strain Poor or irregular sleep Blood sugar swings from skipped meals or high-sugar snacks Environmental toxins like smoke or chemicals Hormone shifts, for example around cycles or life stages These triggers rarely act alone. A few “small” stressors happening at the same time can push the immune system over its tipping point. This is why we do not want to chase each symptom by itself. A root-cause view helps us understand how all these pieces connect for you.The Functional Medicine Roadmap to Cooling Inflammation Our process starts with a deep health story, not a quick intake. We take time to understand patterns across your life and health history, including: Childhood health and past infections Gut symptoms, even if they seem minor Energy patterns throughout the day Exposure to mold, chemicals, or heavy metals Stress history and resilience tools you already use From there, we use targeted lab testing to look at systems, not just single organs. We may explore gut health, nutrient levels, immune markers, and signs of toxic burden. For people trying to reverse autoimmune disease in Boulder, we also think about altitude, outdoor sports, dry air, and local allergens as part of the picture. The aim is to create a clear map of your personal triggers. That map may include patterns such as gut permeability and microbiome imbalance, chronic or hidden infections, toxin exposure from home, hobbies, or work, or mitochondrial dysfunction that affects energy and repair. With that map, we can build a step-by-step plan designed to lower flare frequency and reduce how intense flares feel when they do happen.Natural Strategies That Help You Feel Like Yourself Again Food is one of the clearest ways to talk to the immune system. We often use: Anti-inflammatory eating patterns with plenty of whole, colorful foods Short-term elimination and careful reintroduction of common triggers Blood sugar balance through regular meals with protein, fat, and fiber Tailored guidelines that match your diagnosis and lifestyle Lifestyle shifts are just as important, because inflammation, immune regulation, sleep, and stress response all influence one another. We work with you on: Sleep routines that help your body repair at night Gentle nervous system practices like breathwork or simple relaxation tools Movement plans that respect fatigue and joint pain while keeping you active Stress resilience that fits an active Colorado lifestyle, not one that fights it Supplements can play a helpful role when they are based on data, not trends. For example, we might consider vitamin D, omega-3 fats, or specific herbs only after reviewing your lab work and symptoms. The goal is to support immune balance without guesswork or huge, confusing supplement piles.Remote Care Options to Support Autoimmune Health in Boulder Many people with autoimmune conditions find travel draining, especially during a flare. Because our care is 100 percent remote, people in Boulder and across Colorado can work with a functional medicine doctor from home. No drive in traffic, no sitting in waiting rooms when your body is already worn out. Virtual visits can include: Long, face-to-face video consults to review your history Screen-sharing of lab results so you can see and understand your numbers Health coaching to help you apply the plan in daily life Secure messaging for questions and adjustments between visits Remote care also makes it easier to stick with a long-term plan. We can check in more often through the seasons, adjust protocols if spring pollen or fall smoke brings a change in symptoms, and keep you moving forward instead of starting over after each flare.How Dr. Autoimmune Builds Your Personalized Spring Reset Plan At Dr. Autoimmune, new patients start with a detailed intake and a clear conversation about goals. We combine that story with functional lab testing to understand what your immune system is responding to. Together, we create a care plan that focuses on real, steady change instead of quick band-aids. For springtime in Colorado, that might include: Targeted allergy and sinus support Guidance on pacing outdoor activities and recovery time Plans for handling social events, travel, and changing schedules Practical tools for sleep and stress during light-filled evenings Our team’s goal is to give you skills, education, and ongoing support so you feel more in charge of your health. When you understand your triggers and have a plan you believe in, spring can feel less like something to brace for and more like a season you can enjoy with more confidence and ease.Take the First Step Toward Calming Your Autoimmune Symptoms If you are ready to explore a more comprehensive, root-cause approach to your health, we invite you to see how we help patients reverse autoimmune disease in Boulder. At Dr. Autoimmune, we take time to understand your unique history, triggers, and goals so your care plan is truly individualized. To discuss your symptoms and see whether our approach is a good fit, you can contact us to schedule a consultation.Ready to Find Your Root Cause?Book a discovery call and talk through your symptoms with our team, no obligation.Book your Discovery CallRecent BlogsRoot Causes of Anemia and Low FerritinSeptember 10, 2026Leaky Gut Signs, Causes, and Functional FixesAugust 26, 2026POTS Treatment: Looking Beyond Salt and Medications with Functional MedicineAugust 12, 2026Autoimmune Thyroid Symptoms When TSH Looks NormalJuly 31, 2026View All PostsAt Dr. Autoimmune, we provide personalized, root-cause care to uncover the source of your symptoms and support long-term wellness.+1 (303) 882-8447npc@drautoimmune.comBoulder, CO· Nationwide remote careBook your Discovery Call→Quick LinksHomeAbout UsFeatured InterviewsBlogLearnAreas We ServeLive Webinar ScheduleStoreContact UsShopServicesBook New Patient EvaluationConditions We SupportWellness ServicesPatient PortalPatient StoriesBook An AppointmentConditionsThyroid ConditionsHashimoto's ThyroiditisGraves DiseaseRheumatoid ArthritisType 1 DiabetesInflammatory Bowel DiseaseCeliac & Gluten IntoleranceMultiple Sclerosis© 2026 Dr. Autoimmune. results.bodyText: +1 (303) 882-8447npc@drautoimmune.comHomeAbout UsServicesConditionsPatient StoriesBlogShopContact UsBook your Discovery CallBlogSigns Your Gut May Be Driving Autoimmune FlaresApril 12, 2026•7 minutesWhen Your Gut Sabotages Your Immune System Your gut and your immune system are not separate teams. They share the same field. A large share of your immune cells live in and around your gut, watching what comes in and deciding what is safe or unsafe. When that gut environment is irritated or out of balance, the immune system can start to overreact, which is a real problem if you are already living with an autoimmune condition. Autoimmune flares can feel random, but they often are not. Gut imbalances like dysbiosis, leaky gut, infections, or food sensitivities can quietly build up stress on the immune system. Then something tips the balance: a new food, a period of stress, a poor night of sleep, or a change in routine. Mid-spring often brings all of these at once, with more outdoor time, shifting diets, and seasonal allergies adding extra pressure. At Dr. Autoimmune, we focus on finding these root gut triggers using detailed history, testing, and personalised, fully remote wellness plans, so your care can fit your life wherever you are.Hidden Gut Symptoms That Signal Immune Trouble Some gut symptoms are very clear red flags. If your digestion changes in the days or weeks before a flare, your body may be trying to warn you. Common signs include: Bloating or gas after meals Constipation or needing to strain Loose stools or diarrhoea Abdominal pain or cramping Reflux, heartburn, or a sour taste in the mouth Alternating constipation and diarrhoea These changes can show up before joint pain, rashes, fatigue, or brain fog get worse. The pattern might be subtle, which is why many people miss it. There are also quieter gut clues that still matter for autoimmune conditions: Feeling overly full after a few bites of food Foul-smelling stools or gas Undigested food in the stool Needing frequent antacids or reflux tablets These may point to low stomach acid, poor enzyme output, or an imbalance in gut bacteria. Over time, that can mean poor breakdown of food, irritation of the gut lining, and more immune reactivity. Certain digestive patterns often link with specific autoimmune issues. For example, irritable bowels with bloating can show up alongside joint pain in conditions like rheumatoid-type patterns. Reflux might sit together with skin flares such as psoriasis. Diarrhoea, constipation, and feeling cold or tired may appear with thyroid autoimmunity. Everyone is different, but these clusters are common. One simple step is to track digestive symptoms next to your flare dates. A small notebook or an app can work. Note: What you ate How your gut felt Sleep quality Stress level Any autoimmune symptoms Over time, this can help you and a clinician see patterns and adjust a plan earlier, rather than chasing flares after they hit.Surprising Non-Gut Signs Your Gut Is Struggling Gut stress does not always show up in the toilet. Often it appears on your skin first. Skin acts as a mirror for what is going on inside. Signs that your gut may be involved include: Eczema patches that come and go Psoriasis plaques that flare without a clear reason Rosacea, flushing, or visible small vessels on the face Acne along the jawline or around the mouth Hives or unexplained itching Brain and mood symptoms can also point toward gut trouble. The gut makes and manages many of the chemicals that affect mood and focus. If the gut is inflamed or the microbiome is out of balance, you may notice: Brain fog or feeling slow Anxiety or feeling on edge Low mood or lack of motivation Poor concentration or word-finding issues Headaches or migraines Trouble falling or staying asleep Energy and metabolism can shift as gut health changes. Gut-driven inflammation can affect blood sugar, hormones, and how your body uses fuel. Common signs include: Weight gain or loss without big diet changes Crashes in the afternoon, often with sugar cravings Feeling wired at night but exhausted in the morning Shaky or irritable if meals are delayed As pollen counts rise in spring and people spend more time outside, allergies, sinus pressure, or asthma can flare too. If the gut barrier is already compromised, immune cells may react even more strongly to pollen, dust, or mould, especially in people with existing autoimmunity. Many people in places like Boulder, where there are strong seasonal shifts, notice a clear pattern here.How Gut Imbalances Trigger Autoimmune Flares You may have heard the term leaky gut. The more accurate phrase is increased intestinal permeability. The gut lining is made of tightly joined cells that decide what gets into your bloodstream. When those tight junctions loosen, larger food particles, toxins, and microbes can slip through. Your immune system sees these as threats and attacks them. In people prone to autoimmunity, that repeated alarm can add fuel to flares. Another key piece is dysbiosis, which means the mix of gut bacteria is off. Helpful microbes may be low, while more aggressive ones grow. There can also be: Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, sometimes called SIBO Yeast or fungal overgrowth Parasites or stealth bacterial infections These issues can drive gas, bloating, and pain, but they can also create chemicals that travel in the blood, irritate tissues, and keep the immune system on high alert. Everyday habits can stress the gut too. Chronic stress, poor sleep, frequent use of some medicines like non-steroid anti-inflammatory drugs and long-term acid blockers, ultra-processed foods, and high alcohol intake can all disturb the microbiome and irritate the gut lining. Over time, that can raise inflammation and autoantibody activity. A gut health specialist in Boulder, Colorado, such as our team at Dr. Autoimmune, looks at this full picture. That usually includes in-depth history, targeted testing, personalised nutrition guidance, specific supplements where appropriate, and lifestyle shifts to calm the immune system rather than simply mute symptoms.Resetting Your Gut to Reduce Springtime Flares You cannot control everything around you, but you can give your gut a gentler environment. Seasonally, many people start to eat lighter in spring, which can support gut repair if done with care. Helpful ideas include: Focus on fresh, colourful vegetables, especially leafy and bitter greens Choose whole foods over ultra-processed snacks If you tolerate them, add small amounts of fermented foods like sauerkraut or kefir Reduce added sugars and limit alcohol, which can irritate the gut and feed yeast Habits are just as important as the foods themselves. Gentle gut-supportive practices include: Eating without screens or rushing, and chewing slowly Drinking enough water across the day, not all at once Gradually increasing fibre rather than jumping in quickly Adding light movement, like daily walks in nature, to support bowel motility and stress relief Some people, with medical guidance, try short experiments like removing common trigger foods for a period, such as gluten, dairy, or highly processed foods. The goal is not a perfect diet, but to notice whether joint pain, skin issues, or fatigue shift. Changes in a flare pattern can offer clues about what your immune system reacts to. Self-directed changes can help, but they are usually only one piece of the puzzle, especially if you have had autoimmune flares for years or have several conditions at once. Working with a clinician who understands gut and immune links, whether locally or through remote care, allows for a plan that is tailored to your body, your environment, and your goals, and that is adjusted as you change.Taking Charge of Your Gut, Immune Future Autoimmune flares often feel sudden and out of the blue, but there is usually a story behind them. The gut is a major part of that story. When the gut lining, microbiome, and immune system inside your gut are supported, your whole body can feel calmer and more stable. Digestive quirks, skin changes, brain fog, and energy swings are not just annoyances to push through. They are messages. When we listen to them, we can identify patterns and root causes that typical symptom-focused care may miss. At Dr. Autoimmune, we focus on that deeper gut-immune work as a functional and integrative partner, offering 100 percent remote support so location is not a barrier, even though we are known as a gut health specialist in Boulder, Colorado. By paying attention to the signs your gut is sending, you can take more informed steps toward fewer flares and a steadier life with autoimmunity.Take The Next Step Towards Calmer, Healthier Digestion If you are ready to understand what your gut is really telling you and move beyond short-term fixes, we are here to help. As a dedicated gut health specialist in Boulder, Colorado, Dr. Autoimmune focuses on uncovering root causes and creating practical, personalised plans.
