results.bodyText: +1 (303) 882-8447npc@drautoimmune.comHomeAbout UsServicesConditionsPatient StoriesBlogShopContact UsBook your Discovery CallBlogLeaky Gut Signs, Causes, and Functional FixesAugust 26, 2026•7 minutesWhy Your Gut May Be Leaking and Why No One Mentioned It The term “leaky gut” sounds dramatic, but at its core, it describes a simple concept. Your small intestine is lined with a thin layer of cells that act like a smart coffee filter, allowing nutrients to pass through while keeping larger, potentially irritating particles out. With leaky gut, also known as increased intestinal permeability, that protective barrier becomes more porous. Food particles, bacteria, and toxins can slip into the bloodstream, triggering an immune response. In a healthy gut, tight junctions between cells open and close in a controlled way. Digestion breaks food down into very small components, allowing nutrients to be absorbed without provoking the immune system. When the lining becomes irritated over time, those tight junctions can loosen. Instead of acting as a selective barrier, the gut becomes more like a screen door with several broken sections, allowing unwanted substances to pass through and potentially affect the entire body. Many conventional medical visits focus on labeling and managing symptoms rather than asking why those symptoms developed in the first place. If your lab work appears “normal” and you are not experiencing severe weight loss or bleeding, leaky gut may never even be discussed. You may simply be told your symptoms are IBS, stress, or part of getting older. At Dr. Autoimmune, we view leaky gut as an important piece of the root-cause puzzle, especially when autoimmune conditions and chronic digestive symptoms are involved. For many people, this can appear as persistent bloating, gas, brain fog, joint stiffness, skin flare-ups, fatigue that doesn’t match their lifestyle, or autoimmune symptoms that seem to come out of nowhere. When we recognize the gut as a central control center for immune health, these seemingly unrelated symptoms begin to make sense. The Hidden Triggers That Quietly Damage Your Gut Lining Leaky gut rarely develops overnight. It is usually the result of multiple daily habits and environmental exposures that slowly weaken the intestinal barrier. Highly processed foods, refined sugars, unhealthy oils, and frequent fast food can irritate the intestinal lining while feeding harmful bacteria. For people with sensitivities, gluten may also contribute to ongoing inflammation. Alcohol is another commonly overlooked contributor. Regular alcohol consumption can increase intestinal permeability while disrupting the balance of healthy bacteria. Add chronic stress and poor sleep, and the gut becomes even more vulnerable. When the body remains in a constant fight-or-flight state, digestion slows, blood flow to the intestines decreases, and the body’s ability to repair the gut lining is compromised. Certain medications may also contribute to gut dysfunction. Frequent use of NSAIDs, repeated rounds of antibiotics, and long-term acid-blocking medications can all alter the gut environment. While antibiotics are often necessary, they eliminate beneficial bacteria along with harmful organisms. Acid blockers may also interfere with proper digestion by reducing stomach acid, allowing undesirable microbes to survive and reach the intestines. Hidden infections, environmental toxins, mold exposure, and food sensitivities may further damage the intestinal barrier over time. This is why our functional medicine team looks beyond basic lab work to identify the underlying factors contributing to chronic digestive symptoms. Want to Learn More About Healing Leaky Gut? If you’re wondering whether a leaky gut could be contributing to digestive problems, chronic inflammation, or autoimmune symptoms, we’d love to help you better understand the connection. Join Dr. Ian Hollaman, DC, MSc, FMCP,for our next FREE LIVE Educational Webinaron Wednesday, September 2, at 5:00 PM Mountain Time, where he’ll explain how leaky gut develops, why it matters, and how functional medicine addresses the underlying causes rather than simply masking symptoms. During this webinar, you’ll learn: What leaky gut is and why it matters How increased intestinal permeability may contribute to inflammation and autoimmune conditions Common triggers that can damage the gut lining Functional medicine strategies that support gut healing and long-term wellness Reserve your FREE spot by registering here. How Leaky Gut Fuels Autoimmunity and Inflammation When the gut lining becomes compromised, larger food fragments, bacterial toxins, and other unwanted particles can pass into the bloodstream. Your immune system recognizes these substances as foreign and begins mounting an inflammatory response. If this process continues day after day, inflammation can become chronic. Over time, chronic inflammation may contribute to autoimmune conditions. At Dr. Autoimmune, we commonly work with individuals living with Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, and other autoimmune disorders. In many cases, the immune system gradually loses its ability to distinguish between harmful invaders and healthy tissue. Increased intestinal permeability may contribute to this ongoing immune confusion. The effects often extend far beyond digestion. Chronic inflammation can contribute to brain fog, anxiety, low mood, hormone imbalances, skin conditions, joint discomfort, and persistent fatigue. One of the most important concepts in functional medicine is immune tolerance. A healthy immune system knows when to respond and when to remain calm. Supporting the gut barrier helps reduce unnecessary immune activation and allows the immune system to function more appropriately. What Your Regular Doctor May Be Missing Many people with leaky gut spend years searching for answers. Short office visits often leave little time to discuss nutrition, stress, environmental exposures, or digestive health. When standard laboratory work appears normal, patients are frequently told that everything looks fine despite ongoing symptoms. Important questions are often overlooked, including: Processed food intake Daily sugar consumption Chronic stress Blood sugar regulation Gut microbiome diversity Traditional treatments often focus on symptom relief using medications such as antacids, laxatives, steroids, or immune-suppressing drugs. While these treatments may provide temporary relief, they rarely address why the gut became damaged in the first place. At Dr. Autoimmune, Dr. Ian Hollaman and our team take a more investigative approach. We use advanced stool testing, inflammatory markers, food sensitivity testing, and specialized laboratory evaluations to identify the underlying contributors affecting your digestive and immune health. Instead, functional medicine follows a structured approach that focuses on identifying and correcting the underlying problems. Our approach generally follows four simple steps: Remove harmful triggers such as processed foods, inflammatory foods, infections, or medications when appropriate. Replace digestive support that may be lacking, including stomach acid, digestive enzymes, or bile support. Reinoculate the gut with beneficial bacteria using targeted probiotics and prebiotic nutrition. Repair the intestinal lining with nutrients and lifestyle strategies that support healing. Nutrition remains the foundation of treatment. We typically recommend an anti-inflammatory eating plan centered around whole, nutrient-dense foods while temporarily removing foods that testing or symptoms suggest may be problematic. Specific nutritional supplements, targeted probiotics, and gut-supportive nutrients may be recommended depending on each patient’s needs. Lifestyle also plays a significant role. Sleep quality, stress management, regular movement, and healthy daily habits all influence how well the gut can repair itself. Every care plan is personalized to fit each individual’s lifestyle, health history, and goals. Persistent bloating, alternating constipation and diarrhea, chronic fatigue, food sensitivities, and autoimmune flare-ups should not be ignored. results.bodyText: +1 (303) 882-8447npc@drautoimmune.comHomeAbout UsServicesConditionsPatient StoriesBlogShopContact UsBook your Discovery CallBlogRoot Causes of Anemia and Low FerritinSeptember 10, 2026•8 minutesWhy You Can Be “Anemic” Even When Your Doctor Says Your Iron Is Fine Fatigue that doesn’t improve with sleep. Hair falling out in the shower. Cold hands, brittle nails, brain fog, and a heart that races when you climb the stairs. Many people living with these symptoms are told their bloodwork is “normal,” only to keep feeling worse. In our experience at Dr. Autoimmune, one of the most commonly missed pieces of this puzzle is low ferritin, the body’s stored form of iron, even when a standard complete blood count (CBC) looks acceptable. Anemia is not a diagnosis in itself. It is a sign that something upstream is off, whether that’s absorption, chronic inflammation, blood loss, thyroid function, or an autoimmune process quietly running in the background. Conventional visits often stop once hemoglobin falls within a wide reference range. Ferritin, iron saturation, total iron-binding capacity, and the deeper “why” behind the numbers are frequently left unexamined. At Dr. Autoimmune, we treat anemia and low ferritin as a starting point for investigation, not an endpoint. If your labs look borderline, your iron supplement isn’t working, or you’ve been told your fatigue is “just stress,” this article walks through the root causes we look for and how a functional medicine approach differs from simply refilling an iron prescription. Want to Learn More About the Root Causes of Anemia and Low Ferritin? If you’re struggling with fatigue, brain fog, low energy, or low ferritin—even when you’ve been told your iron levels are “normal”—we’d love to help you better understand what may be going on. Join Dr. Ian Hollaman, DC, MSc, FMCP, for our next FREE LIVE Educational Webinar on Wednesday, September 16, at 5:00 PM Mountain Time, where he’ll explain why anemia and low ferritin develop, what routine labs may miss, and how a functional medicine approach looks beyond the numbers to uncover potential underlying causes. During this webinar, you’ll learn: What ferritin actually measures and why “normal” ranges can still leave you symptomatic How gut health, chronic inflammation, and autoimmune activity can affect iron absorption and storage Common root causes of low ferritin that are frequently overlooked Functional medicine strategies that support healthy iron levels and long-term energy Reserve your FREE spot by registering here.Ferritin 101: The Difference Between “Iron” and “Stored Iron” Most people only hear about “iron” in the context of red blood cells, but ferritin tells a different part of the story. Ferritin is the protein that stores iron inside your cells for later use, essentially your body’s iron savings account. Serum iron and hemoglobin reflect what’s circulating right now, while ferritin reflects your reserves. This distinction matters clinically. Ferritin can drop for months, sometimes years, before hemoglobin or a standard CBC ever flags a problem. By the time hemoglobin is low enough to be labeled “anemia,” the underlying iron depletion has often been building for a long time. This is why so many people feel exhausted, foggy, and unwell while being told their labs are unremarkable; the test that would catch the problem early, ferritin, is frequently left off the standard panel altogether. It’s also worth noting that ferritin is an acute-phase reactant, meaning it can rise in response to inflammation, even when true iron stores are low. This is one reason ferritin should never be interpreted alone. A thorough evaluation typically pairs ferritin with iron, total iron-binding capacity (TIBC), transferrin saturation, and inflammatory markers like CRP, so the full picture, not just one number, guides the plan. The Root Causes Behind Low Ferritin and Anemia Low ferritin rarely has a single cause. In our clinic, we look across several systems at once to understand why your body isn’t holding onto or absorbing enough iron. 1. Poor Gut Absorption and Digestive Dysfunction Iron is absorbed primarily in the small intestine, and that process depends on adequate stomach acid and a healthy intestinal lining. Low stomach acid, chronic use of acid-blocking medications, increased intestinal permeability (leaky gut), and small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) can all interfere with how much iron actually makes it into your bloodstream, no matter how much you’re eating or supplementing. 2. Celiac Disease and Gluten-Related Gut Damage Unexplained iron-deficiency anemia is one of the most common presenting signs of celiac disease and gluten sensitivity. Ongoing gluten exposure in a sensitive person damages the villi lining the small intestine, the same tissue responsible for absorbing iron, B12, and folate. Anemia that doesn’t respond to supplementation is a classic reason we screen for celiac disease and non-celiac gluten sensitivity. 3. Chronic Inflammation and Autoimmune Activity Persistent inflammation triggers the release of a hormone called hepcidin, which blocks iron from being absorbed in the gut and locks existing iron away in storage instead of releasing it for use. This pattern, known as anemia of chronic disease, is common in people with inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, and other autoimmune conditions. It’s a key reason ferritin can look “normal” or even elevated on paper while true iron availability to your tissues stays low. 4. Thyroid Dysfunction Thyroid hormone helps regulate stomach acid production and red blood cell formation. When thyroid function is low, or when autoimmune thyroid disease is present even with a normal TSH, iron metabolism often suffers alongside it. We frequently see low ferritin and sluggish thyroid function occurring together, each one making the other harder to resolve until both are addressed. 5. Heavy Menstrual Cycles and Unrecognized Blood Loss Heavy or prolonged periods, fibroids, and slow gastrointestinal blood loss (from ulcers, hemorrhoids, or inflammatory conditions) are straightforward but frequently overlooked contributors to falling ferritin. Because this blood loss can be gradual, it’s easy to underestimate just how much iron is being lost over time. 6. Diet, Nutrient Cofactors, and Absorption Blockers Low intake of iron-rich foods, especially in vegetarian and vegan diets, plays a role, but it’s rarely the whole story. Iron absorption also depends on adequate vitamin C, B12, copper, and stomach acid. Frequent coffee or tea with meals, high-calcium supplements taken alongside iron, and certain medications can all blunt how much iron your body actually takes up. 7. Chronic Stress, Poor Sleep, and Blood Sugar Swings Chronic stress and unstable blood sugar keep the body in a heightened inflammatory state, which, as noted above, can suppress iron absorption through the same hepcidin pathway. Poor sleep further limits the body’s capacity for tissue repair and healthy red blood cell turnover.What a Standard Iron Panel Often Misses Many people are told their iron is “fine” after a CBC alone, or after ferritin is checked once without the surrounding context. Questions that are often left unasked include: Is ferritin being interpreted alongside inflammatory markers, or in isolation? Has celiac disease or gluten sensitivity ever been ruled out? Is there an undiagnosed autoimmune or thyroid condition driving chronic inflammation? Is stomach acid adequate, and are digestive symptoms being taken seriously? Is menstrual blood loss, or another source of ongoing blood loss, being accounted for? Standard care often responds to low iron with a generic supplement and a recheck in a few months. When levels don’t improve, or symptoms persist despite “normal” numbers, that is usually a sign the underlying driver hasn’t been identified yet, not that the anemia is imaginary. At Dr. Autoimmune, we use expanded lab panels, including ferritin, iron saturation, TIBC, inflammatory markers, B12, folate, and thyroid antibodies where appropriate, to see the full picture rather than a single data point. Learn more about the conditions we support and how root-cause testing fits into your overall care.A Functional Medicine Roadmap for Anemia and Low Ferritin Correcting low ferritin isn’t just about taking more iron. Our approach generally follows four steps: Test thoroughly, looking beyond hemoglobin to ferritin, iron saturation, TIBC, inflammatory markers, and relevant nutrient and thyroid panels to understand the full pattern. Identify the underlying driver, whether that’s gut absorption, celiac disease, autoimmune inflammation, thyroid dysfunction, or ongoing blood loss. Replenish iron stores using a form and dose appropriate to your gut tolerance and absorption capacity, paired with supportive nutrients like vitamin C, B12, and folate as needed. Repair the systems that allowed ferritin to drop in the first place, supporting gut healing, calming autoimmune activity, and optimizing thyroid and blood sugar balance so your levels stay stable long-term. Nutrition remains foundational. We typically recommend nutrient-dense, anti-inflammatory eating patterns rich in well-absorbed iron sources, while identifying and temporarily removing foods that testing or symptoms suggest may be problematic, such as gluten in the case of confirmed sensitivity or celiac disease. Every plan is personalized based on your labs, symptoms, and history, since the right approach for someone with Hashimoto’s thyroiditis will look different from the right approach for someone with heavy menstrual cycles or undiagnosed celiac disease.Why the Gut-Immune Connection Matters Here Too Because so many root causes of low ferritin trace back to the gut and immune system, we often evaluate anemia alongside broader gut and autoimmune health. If you’d like to understand this connection in more depth, our articles on the hidden link between gut health and autoimmune disease and leaky gut signs, causes, and functional fixes walk through how a compromised gut lining can quietly drive inflammation throughout the body, iron metabolism included.Take the Next Step Toward Understanding Your Fatigue Join our upcoming FREE LIVE Educational Webinar onWednesday, September 16 at 5:00 PM Mountain Time, where Dr. Ian Hollaman, DC, MSc, FMCP will explain the root causes of anemia and low ferritin, why routine labs may not always tell the full story, and how a functional medicine approach. looks deeper to identify factors affecting iron absorption and storage. If you’re ready to move beyond a generic iron supplement and get real answers, our team at Dr. Autoimmune is here to help. We’ll review your health history, evaluate your complete iron and inflammatory picture, and build a personalized plan designed to restore your energy and support long-term wellness. jsonLdParsed.description: Certain medications can trigger a positive ANA test or drug-induced lupus. Learn which drugs are most commonly linked and what to do if this affects you.

mainEntity.name: Will my ANA test go back to normal if I stop the medication?

acceptedAnswer.text: In many documented cases of drug-induced ANA positivity or drug-induced lupus, antibody levels and symptoms do improve after the triggering medication is discontinued under medical guidance, though this can take weeks to months and should always be monitored by your provider.

mainEntity.name: Can supplements cause a positive ANA test?

acceptedAnswer.text: Drug-induced ANA positivity is best documented with prescription medications rather than typical over-the-counter supplements. If you're taking supplements alongside prescription medications, it's still worth listing everything for your provider so nothing is overlooked when interpreting your results.

mainEntity.name: Should I stop taking my medication if my ANA test is positive?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not without speaking to your prescribing provider first. Many of the medications associated with ANA positivity treat serious underlying conditions, so any change should be a shared decision based on your full health picture, not made independently.

jsonLdParsed.description: What does an ANA titer of 1:80, 1:160, or 1:320 actually mean? Learn how ANA titer levels are read, why a higher number isn't always worse, and next steps.

mainEntity.name: Does a 1:320 ANA titer mean I have lupus?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. A 1:320 titer means your ANA test is positive at a relatively high dilution, but ANA positivity alone isn't specific to lupus. Many people with a high titer never have any autoimmune diagnosis, while lupus itself is diagnosed using a combination of symptoms, additional antibody tests, and clinical criteria — not titer level alone.

mainEntity.name: Can a positive ANA titer go back to normal?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, titers can fluctuate over time and with treatment of an underlying trigger, and some people's ANA reverts to negative. Others remain ANA-positive indefinitely without ever developing symptoms, which is why titer trends are usually interpreted alongside your clinical picture rather than on their own.

mainEntity.name: What staining patterns are reported with an ANA titer?

acceptedAnswer.text: Common patterns include homogeneous, speckled, nucleolar, and centromere, each associated with different underlying antibody targets. The pattern is reported alongside the titer and can help guide which follow-up antibody tests your provider orders next.

results.bodyText: +1 (303) 882-8447npc@drautoimmune.comHomeAbout UsServicesConditionsPatient StoriesBlogShopContact UsBook your Discovery CallANA Titer Levels Explained: What Do 1:80, 1:160, and 1:320 Mean?Lab Results ExplainedA positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) test is reported as a titer, not just “positive” or “negative.” Here's how to read that number.Home/Learn/ANA Titer Levels Explained: What Do 1:80, 1:160, and 1:320 Mean?If your antinuclear antibody (ANA) test came back positive, the lab report likely included a ratio like 1:80, 1:160, or 1:320 alongside a staining pattern (such as speckled or homogeneous). That ratio is called the titer, and understanding what it means — and what it doesn't — can make a confusing result much easier to sit with while you wait for follow-up care.This isn't a diagnosis on its own. A positive ANA test tells your provider that your immune system is producing antibodies against components of your own cell nuclei, but it doesn't say which condition (if any) is causing that, or how severe it is.How the ANA Titer Number Is DeterminedIn the lab, your blood sample is diluted step by step — 1:40, 1:80, 1:160, 1:320, and so on — and examined under a fluorescence microscope at each dilution to see how far it can be diluted before the antibody staining is no longer visible.A titer of 1:320 means the antibodies were still detectable even after your sample was diluted much more than a sample with a titer of 1:80. In general, a higher titer indicates a greater concentration of antinuclear antibodies in the blood — but it does not automatically mean a more serious condition or worse symptoms.Is a Higher Titer Always More Concerning?Not necessarily. Titer level is one piece of a much larger picture that includes your symptoms, the specific antibody staining pattern, more detailed antibody panels (such as anti-dsDNA or anti-Smith antibodies), and your overall clinical presentation.It's also common for healthy people, especially women, to have a low-titer positive ANA (often 1:40 or 1:80) with no underlying autoimmune condition at all. Titers of 1:160 or higher are more often followed up with additional testing, but plenty of people with a 1:320 titer never develop an autoimmune disease, while some people with autoimmune symptoms have a lower titer.1:40 – 1:80: Often considered a low-positive result; can occur in healthy individuals.1:160: A moderate titer that's more likely to prompt further antibody testing.1:320 or higher: A higher-positive result that typically warrants a closer clinical review alongside symptoms.What Usually Happens After a Positive ANA TiterYour provider will typically look at your titer together with the staining pattern reported by the lab (homogeneous, speckled, nucleolar, or centromere, among others), order more specific antibody tests if warranted, and review your symptom history — things like joint pain, fatigue, rashes, or unexplained fevers.A root-cause functional medicine approach also looks upstream: at gut health, chronic infections, environmental triggers, and inflammation markers that may be contributing to immune dysregulation, rather than looking at the ANA titer in isolation.Ready for Personalized Answers?General information is a starting point — a Discovery Call helps us look at your specific labs, symptoms, and history to build a plan that's actually yours.Book your Discovery CallFrequently Asked Questions01Does a 1:320 ANA titer mean I have lupus?No. A 1:320 titer means your ANA test is positive at a relatively high dilution, but ANA positivity alone isn't specific to lupus. mainEntity.name: Should I get retested if my ANA is positive but I have no symptoms?

mainEntity.name: Does a viral infection cause a permanent positive ANA?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not usually. ANA elevations related to a recent viral infection are often temporary and can normalize as the infection resolves, though this should still be confirmed with follow-up testing rather than assumed.

Here's what else can cause it.Home/Learn/False Positive ANA Test: What Can Cause It?It's a common (and understandably stressful) experience: an ANA test comes back positive, but there's no clear autoimmune diagnosis to explain it. Before assuming the worst, it helps to know that a meaningful percentage of positive ANA results occur in people without lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, or any other autoimmune condition.“False positive” isn't always the most accurate way to describe these results — the antibody is genuinely present — but it may not reflect an active autoimmune disease. Below are the most well-documented reasons a positive ANA can occur without autoimmune disease being the cause.Common Non-Autoimmune Causes of a Positive ANASeveral factors are well-documented to cause ANA positivity in the absence of an autoimmune diagnosis:Age — ANA positivity becomes more common with age, even in otherwise healthy adults.Being female — women are more likely than men to have a positive ANA without disease.Recent or chronic viral infections — including Epstein-Barr virus, which can transiently trigger ANA positivity.Certain medications — see our related article on medications linked to positive ANA results.A family history of autoimmune disease, even without a diagnosis yourself.Low-titer results (often 1:40 to 1:80), which are more likely to occur without underlying disease than higher titers.Why Titer and Pattern Matter for InterpretationA low-titer ANA in someone with no symptoms is interpreted very differently than a high-titer ANA in someone with joint pain, unexplained rashes, and fatigue. The staining pattern reported by the lab, along with more specific antibody panels, helps your provider judge how likely the result is to reflect true autoimmune disease versus an incidental finding.This is why a positive ANA test is rarely acted on in isolation — it's one data point that's weighed against your full symptom picture and additional labs.What a Root-Cause Approach Looks At NextRather than treating a positive ANA as an endpoint, a functional medicine evaluation looks upstream at what might be driving immune activation in the first place — gut health and intestinal permeability, chronic low-grade infections, environmental exposures, nutrient deficiencies, and chronic stress — alongside conventional antibody testing.Ready for Personalized Answers?General information is a starting point — a Discovery Call helps us look at your specific labs, symptoms, and history to build a plan that's actually yours.Book your Discovery CallFrequently Asked Questions01Can a healthy person have a positive ANA test?Yes. mainEntity.name: Is autoimmune hepatitis the same as regular hepatitis?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Viral hepatitis (like hepatitis A, B, or C) is caused by a virus, while autoimmune hepatitis occurs when the immune system attacks the liver itself, without a viral infection as the trigger. They require different diagnostic testing and treatment approaches.

mainEntity.name: Can autoimmune hepatitis cause itching without a visible rash?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Itching related to liver inflammation (often from changes in bile acid processing) can occur without an obvious visible rash, which is one reason unexplained itching alongside fatigue or abdominal discomfort is worth mentioning to a provider.

mainEntity.name: Does autoimmune hepatitis often occur with other autoimmune conditions?

acceptedAnswer.text: It can. Autoimmune hepatitis is sometimes seen alongside other autoimmune conditions, such as thyroid disease or inflammatory bowel disease, which is why a broader evaluation of symptoms and antibody patterns is often useful rather than looking at the liver in isolation.

results.bodyText: +1 (303) 882-8447npc@drautoimmune.comHomeAbout UsServicesConditionsPatient StoriesBlogShopContact UsBook your Discovery CallAutoimmune Hepatitis Symptoms and Skin Rash: What to KnowConditions EducationAutoimmune hepatitis is a lesser-known autoimmune condition affecting the liver, and some people also notice skin changes alongside their symptoms.Home/Learn/Autoimmune Hepatitis Symptoms and Skin Rash: What to KnowAutoimmune hepatitis occurs when the immune system mistakenly attacks the liver, causing inflammation that, if untreated, can progress over time. It's less commonly discussed than conditions like Hashimoto's or rheumatoid arthritis, but it shares the same underlying pattern: the immune system targeting healthy tissue.Because early symptoms can be vague or overlap with other conditions, autoimmune hepatitis is sometimes discovered through routine blood work showing elevated liver enzymes before more noticeable symptoms appear.Common Symptoms of Autoimmune HepatitisSymptoms vary widely between individuals and can range from barely noticeable to significant. Commonly reported symptoms include:Persistent fatigueJoint pain or achingNausea or loss of appetiteAbdominal discomfort, particularly upper right sideJaundice (yellowing of the skin or eyes) in more advanced casesDark urine or pale stoolsSkin changes, including rash or itching (pruritus)The Skin Rash and Autoimmune Hepatitis ConnectionSkin symptoms in autoimmune hepatitis can occur for a few different reasons. Itching (pruritus) is a well-documented symptom linked to how the liver processes bile acids when inflamed. Some people also develop a rash as part of an overlapping autoimmune condition, since autoimmune hepatitis can occur alongside other autoimmune diseases (a pattern sometimes called autoimmune polyendocrine or overlap syndrome).Because skin changes have many possible causes, a rash alone isn't enough to diagnose autoimmune hepatitis — it's typically evaluated alongside liver function tests, specific antibody testing (such as ANA, anti-smooth muscle antibody, or anti-LKM1), and sometimes a liver biopsy.How Autoimmune Hepatitis Is Typically Evaluated and SupportedDiagnosis generally involves blood tests for liver enzymes and specific autoantibodies, along with imaging or biopsy when needed. Conventional treatment often includes immunosuppressive medication to control the immune attack on the liver.A root-cause functional medicine approach can complement conventional care by addressing gut health, nutrient status, and inflammatory triggers that may support overall immune regulation — always working alongside, not replacing, appropriate monitoring by a hepatologist or gastroenterologist for this condition.Ready for Personalized Answers?General information is a starting point — a Discovery Call helps us look at your specific labs, symptoms, and history to build a plan that's actually yours.Book your Discovery CallFrequently Asked Questions01Is autoimmune hepatitis the same as regular hepatitis?No. Viral hepatitis (like hepatitis A, B, or C) is caused by a virus, while autoimmune hepatitis occurs when the immune system attacks the liver itself, without a viral infection as the trigger. jsonLdParsed.description: Many people notice autoimmune symptoms worsen during stressful periods. Learn how stress and the immune system are connected and what may help.

mainEntity.name: Can stress alone cause an autoimmune disease?

acceptedAnswer.text: Stress on its own isn't considered a sole cause of autoimmune disease. Most functional medicine and conventional models describe autoimmune disease as arising from a combination of genetic predisposition, environmental triggers, and immune dysregulation — with chronic stress acting as one potential contributing factor rather than a standalone cause.

mainEntity.name: How quickly can stress trigger a flare?

acceptedAnswer.text: This varies significantly by person and condition. Some people notice symptoms worsening within days of a highly stressful event, while for others the connection is only clear when looking back over weeks or months of symptom patterns.

mainEntity.name: What helps calm an autoimmune flare linked to stress?

acceptedAnswer.text: Approaches vary by individual and condition, but commonly discussed strategies include prioritizing consistent sleep, nervous-system regulation practices like breathwork or meditation, gentle movement, and addressing underlying gut or nutrient imbalances — always alongside, not in place of, your prescribed medical treatment plan.

results.bodyText: +1 (303) 882-8447npc@drautoimmune.comHomeAbout UsServicesConditionsPatient StoriesBlogShopContact UsBook your Discovery CallCan Stress Trigger an Autoimmune Disease Flare-Up?Root-Cause EducationIf your symptoms seem to worsen during stressful periods, you're not imagining it — here's how stress and immune function are connected.Home/Learn/Can Stress Trigger an Autoimmune Disease Flare-Up?Many people living with an autoimmune condition notice a pattern: a stressful stretch at work, a major life change, or a period of poor sleep seems to line up with a flare-up of joint pain, fatigue, skin symptoms, or digestive issues. This isn't just a coincidence for most people — there's a well-established biological relationship between chronic stress and immune regulation.Understanding this connection isn't about blaming stress for your condition, or being told to “just relax.” It's about recognizing one modifiable piece of a much larger picture that also includes gut health, nutrition, sleep, and environmental triggers.How Stress and the Immune System Are ConnectedChronic stress activates the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, leading to sustained changes in cortisol and other stress hormones. In the short term, cortisol is anti-inflammatory, but with prolonged stress, immune cells can become less responsive to cortisol's regulating signal — a phenomenon sometimes described as cortisol resistance — which can allow inflammation to persist or increase.Chronic stress is also linked to changes in gut permeability and the gut microbiome, both of which play a role in immune regulation for people with autoimmune conditions. Sleep disruption, which often accompanies chronic stress, independently affects inflammatory markers as well.Signs Stress May Be Contributing to Your SymptomsWhile everyone's pattern is different, some common signs that stress may be playing a role include:Symptom flares that reliably follow high-stress periods (deadlines, grief, major life changes)Sleep disruption alongside worsening joint pain, skin symptoms, or fatigueDigestive symptoms that intensify during anxious or high-pressure periodsSymptom improvement during vacations or lower-stress stretchesA Root-Cause Approach to Stress and Autoimmune SymptomsRather than treating stress management as an afterthought, a functional medicine evaluation looks at stress alongside gut health, sleep quality, nutrient status, and inflammatory triggers as part of the full picture driving your symptoms.This often includes practical strategies like sleep optimization, nervous system regulation techniques (such as breathwork), and addressing underlying gut or nutrient imbalances that may be amplifying your body's stress response — in addition to, not instead of, appropriate medical care for your specific condition.Ready for Personalized Answers?General information is a starting point — a Discovery Call helps us look at your specific labs, symptoms, and history to build a plan that's actually yours.Book your Discovery CallFrequently Asked Questions01Can stress alone cause an autoimmune disease?Stress on its own isn't considered a sole cause of autoimmune disease. mainEntity.name: Does having an MTHFR mutation mean I will develop an autoimmune disease?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. MTHFR gene variants are very common in the general population, and most people who carry one never develop an autoimmune condition. It's considered one potential contributing factor among many, not a predictor or cause on its own.

mainEntity.name: Should everyone with an autoimmune disease get tested for MTHFR?

acceptedAnswer.text: This depends on your individual symptoms and history. Some providers include it as part of a broader root-cause workup, especially when nutrient deficiencies are suspected, while others focus directly on measuring active folate, B12, and homocysteine levels rather than the gene variant itself.

mainEntity.name: Can diet affect MTHFR-related methylation issues?

acceptedAnswer.text: Diet and targeted supplementation with active forms of folate and B12 (rather than synthetic folic acid) are commonly discussed strategies for supporting methylation in people with reduced MTHFR enzyme activity, but any supplementation should be guided by your actual lab results and a qualified provider.

results.bodyText: +1 (303) 882-8447npc@drautoimmune.comHomeAbout UsServicesConditionsPatient StoriesBlogShopContact UsBook your Discovery CallMTHFR Gene Mutation and Autoimmune Disease: What's the Connection?Root-Cause EducationMTHFR is one of the most talked-about genes in functional medicine. Here's what it actually does, and why it's often discussed alongside autoimmune conditions.Home/Learn/MTHFR Gene Mutation and Autoimmune Disease: What's the Connection?If you've had genetic testing done, or if a functional medicine provider has mentioned “methylation,” you may have come across the term MTHFR. It refers to a gene — methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase — that provides instructions for an enzyme involved in processing folate (vitamin B9) and regulating a process called methylation, which touches nearly every system in the body, including immune function.MTHFR gene variants are extremely common; having one doesn't mean something is inherently wrong. What matters more is understanding what the gene does and whether your individual nutrient status and symptoms suggest it's worth addressing as part of your care.What Does the MTHFR Gene Actually Do?The MTHFR enzyme converts folate into its active, usable form (5-MTHF), which is required for methylation — a chemical process involved in DNA repair, neurotransmitter production, detoxification, and regulation of gene expression, including genes that influence immune cell behavior.Common variants of the MTHFR gene (most notably C677T and A1298C) can reduce the enzyme's efficiency, which may lead to lower levels of active folate and, in some cases, elevated homocysteine — an amino acid linked to inflammation when chronically elevated.Why MTHFR Comes Up in Autoimmune DiscussionsMethylation influences how immune cells communicate and regulate inflammation, which is why some functional medicine providers consider MTHFR variants as one piece of the puzzle in people with autoimmune conditions — particularly when nutrient testing shows low active folate, low B12, or elevated homocysteine alongside ongoing symptoms.It's important to be clear: having an MTHFR variant does not cause autoimmune disease on its own, and most people with an MTHFR variant never develop one. It's one of many factors that may be considered as part of a broader root-cause evaluation, not a diagnosis in itself.What a Root-Cause Evaluation Looks AtRather than testing for MTHFR in isolation, a thorough functional medicine evaluation typically looks at actual nutrient levels (active folate, B12, homocysteine), symptoms, and your broader health picture — since two people with the same gene variant can have very different nutrient statuses and needs.When relevant, support may include dietary changes and targeted supplementation with active forms of folate and B12, always personalized to your labs rather than applied as a blanket recommendation.Ready for Personalized Answers?General information is a starting point — a Discovery Call helps us look at your specific labs, symptoms, and history to build a plan that's actually yours.Book your Discovery CallFrequently Asked Questions01Does having an MTHFR mutation mean I will develop an autoimmune disease?No. MTHFR gene variants are very common in the general population, and most people who carry one never develop an autoimmune condition. jsonLdParsed.description: Rheumatologist, endocrinologist, immunologist, or functional medicine doctor? Learn which specialists treat autoimmune disease and how they differ.

mainEntity.name: Should I see a rheumatologist or a functional medicine doctor first?

acceptedAnswer.text: If you have specific symptoms suggestive of a particular autoimmune condition (like joint swelling or a suspicious rash), a relevant specialist such as a rheumatologist can help confirm or rule out a diagnosis. A functional medicine doctor can be valuable at any point — before, during, or after a formal diagnosis — to address root-cause factors alongside your specialist's care.

mainEntity.name: Can a functional medicine doctor diagnose autoimmune disease?

acceptedAnswer.text: Functional medicine doctors can order and interpret many of the same antibody and inflammatory marker tests used in conventional diagnosis, and can identify patterns suggestive of autoimmune disease. Formal diagnosis of certain conditions may still involve imaging, biopsy, or criteria managed by a relevant specialist.

mainEntity.name: Do I need a referral to see an autoimmune specialist?

acceptedAnswer.text: This depends on your insurance plan and location. Many rheumatologists, endocrinologists, and other specialists require a referral from a primary care provider, while functional medicine practices (including telehealth ones) often allow direct scheduling without a referral.

results.bodyText: +1 (303) 882-8447npc@drautoimmune.comHomeAbout UsServicesConditionsPatient StoriesBlogShopContact UsBook your Discovery CallWhat Type of Doctor Treats Autoimmune Disease?Choosing Your Care TeamAutoimmune conditions can involve several different specialists. Here's a plain-language breakdown of who treats what, and how they work together.Home/Learn/What Type of Doctor Treats Autoimmune Disease?One of the more confusing parts of navigating a possible autoimmune diagnosis is figuring out which type of doctor to see in the first place. Autoimmune diseases can affect nearly any organ system, so the “right” specialist often depends on which condition is suspected and which organs are involved.Many people end up seeing more than one specialist over time, and increasingly, a functional or integrative medicine provider alongside conventional specialists to address root causes rather than symptoms in isolation.Specialists Commonly Involved in Autoimmune CareDepending on your symptoms and suspected condition, your care team might include:Rheumatologist — joint, muscle, and connective tissue conditions like rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, and Sjögren's syndromeEndocrinologist — hormone-related autoimmune conditions such as Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Graves' disease, and type 1 diabetesGastroenterologist — digestive-system autoimmune conditions like celiac disease and inflammatory bowel diseaseImmunologist — complex or overlapping immune dysfunction, especially when multiple systems are involvedNeurologist — autoimmune conditions affecting the nervous system, such as multiple sclerosisDermatologist — autoimmune skin conditions and skin manifestations of systemic diseasePrimary care provider — often the first point of contact and coordinator of referralsFunctional medicine doctor — focuses on identifying and addressing underlying root causes (gut health, triggers, nutrient status) alongside conventional specialty careWhy You Might See More Than One Type of DoctorAutoimmune diseases don't always stay confined to a single organ system, and it's common to have overlapping conditions (for example, Hashimoto's alongside celiac disease). Because of this, many patients work with a primary specialist for their main diagnosis while also incorporating a functional medicine provider to look at gut health, inflammation, and lifestyle factors that conventional specialty visits may not have time to fully address.How a Functional Medicine Doctor Fits InA functional medicine doctor doesn't typically replace a rheumatologist, endocrinologist, or other specialist for disease-specific monitoring and medication management. mainEntity.name: Is telehealth a good option for autoimmune care?

jsonLdParsed.description: Wondering whether to see a rheumatologist or a functional medicine doctor? Here's what each visit typically looks like and how the two approaches differ.

mainEntity.name: Can a functional medicine doctor replace my rheumatologist?

acceptedAnswer.text: For most people with a confirmed autoimmune diagnosis requiring disease-modifying medication, a functional medicine doctor works best as a complement to — not a replacement for — rheumatology care, focusing on root-cause and lifestyle factors alongside your prescribed treatment.

mainEntity.name: How long is a typical functional medicine initial visit compared to a rheumatology visit?

acceptedAnswer.text: Functional medicine initial visits are often longer, sometimes 60-90 minutes, to allow a thorough review of your full history, while rheumatology visits (especially follow-ups) are frequently shorter and focused on disease activity and medication management.

mainEntity.name: Will a functional medicine doctor order the same labs as a rheumatologist?

acceptedAnswer.text: There's often overlap in antibody and inflammatory marker testing, but functional medicine evaluations frequently add nutrient status, gut health, and additional inflammatory markers not always included in a standard rheumatology workup.

Here's what to expect from each.Home/Learn/Functional Medicine vs. Rheumatologist: What to Expect at Each VisitIf you're dealing with joint pain, fatigue, or a suspected autoimmune condition, you may be deciding between (or considering both) a rheumatologist and a functional medicine doctor. Understanding what each visit typically involves can help you set realistic expectations and choose the right starting point for your situation.What to Expect at a Rheumatologist VisitA rheumatologist specializes in diagnosing and managing autoimmune and inflammatory joint conditions, such as rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, and Sjögren's syndrome. A typical visit includes a focused physical exam of your joints, a review of relevant antibody and inflammatory marker labs, and imaging when needed.Treatment often centers on disease-modifying medications and biologics aimed at controlling inflammation and preventing joint damage, with follow-up visits to monitor disease activity and medication response.What to Expect at a Functional Medicine VisitA functional medicine visit for autoimmune or joint-related concerns typically involves a longer initial appointment focused on your complete history — diet, digestion, sleep, stress, past infections, and environmental exposures — alongside comprehensive lab testing that may include nutrient levels, inflammatory markers, and gut health markers in addition to standard antibody panels.The resulting plan usually centers on dietary changes, targeted supplementation, and lifestyle modifications designed to address root-cause contributors to inflammation, alongside (not instead of) any medication prescribed by your other specialists.Choosing Between the Two (or Using Both)These approaches aren't mutually exclusive. Many patients use a rheumatologist for diagnosis, disease monitoring, and medication management, while working with a functional medicine provider on the root-cause and lifestyle side of their care — gut health, nutrition, and inflammation reduction strategies that complement their medical treatment plan.Ready for Personalized Answers?General information is a starting point — a Discovery Call helps us look at your specific labs, symptoms, and history to build a plan that's actually yours.Book your Discovery CallFrequently Asked Questions01Can a functional medicine doctor replace my rheumatologist?For most people with a confirmed autoimmune diagnosis requiring disease-modifying medication, a functional medicine doctor works best as a complement to — not a replacement for — rheumatology care, focusing on root-cause and lifestyle factors alongside your prescribed treatment.02How long is a typical functional medicine initial visit compared to a rheumatology visit?03Will a functional medicine doctor order the same labs as a rheumatologist?Related ReadingRheumatoid ArthritisLupusThis article is for general educational purposes only and is not a substitute for professional medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. jsonLdParsed.description: IBS and autoimmune conditions like IBD can look similar but aren't the same thing. Learn how irritable bowel syndrome differs from autoimmune disease.

mainEntity.name: Can IBS turn into an autoimmune disease over time?

acceptedAnswer.text: IBS itself is not currently understood to progress into an autoimmune disease. However, because IBS-like symptoms can sometimes mask or coexist with an autoimmune digestive condition, persistent or worsening symptoms are worth having properly evaluated rather than assumed to be IBS alone.

mainEntity.name: How can I tell if my symptoms are IBS or something autoimmune, like IBD?

acceptedAnswer.text: Certain “red flag” symptoms — such as blood in the stool, unintended weight loss, nighttime symptoms that wake you up, or fever — are not typical of IBS and warrant prompt evaluation for inflammatory bowel disease or another condition. Inflammatory markers, stool tests, and sometimes colonoscopy can help distinguish the two.

mainEntity.name: Does treating gut health help IBS symptoms even though it's not autoimmune?

acceptedAnswer.text: Many people with IBS do find that addressing gut microbiome balance, food triggers, and stress can meaningfully improve symptoms, even though IBS isn't classified as autoimmune — the gut-brain and gut-microbiome connections play a role in both types of conditions.

Here's how they're actually different.Home/Learn/Is Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) an Autoimmune Disease?Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is one of the most common digestive complaints, and because its symptoms — abdominal pain, bloating, and altered bowel habits — can overlap with autoimmune digestive conditions, it's a fair question: is IBS itself an autoimmune disease?The short answer is no, IBS is not classified as an autoimmune disease. But the two are often discussed together because they can look similar on the surface, sometimes coexist, and both involve gut function — which is worth understanding clearly.IBS vs. Autoimmune Digestive Conditions: The Key DifferenceIBS is classified as a functional gastrointestinal disorder — meaning the digestive tract doesn't work the way it should, causing real symptoms, but without the visible tissue damage or inflammation seen on colonoscopy or biopsy that defines autoimmune conditions like inflammatory bowel disease (IBD, which includes Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis) or celiac disease.Autoimmune digestive conditions involve the immune system actively attacking the digestive tract, which can be confirmed through inflammatory markers, antibody testing, and visible changes on imaging or biopsy. IBS diagnosis, by contrast, is typically made based on symptom patterns after ruling out other conditions, since there isn't a single definitive test for it.Why IBS and Autoimmune Conditions Are Often ConfusedSeveral factors contribute to the overlap in how people think about these conditions:Similar core symptoms: abdominal pain, bloating, and changes in bowel habits appear in both.IBS and IBD can coexist — some people with well-controlled IBD still experience IBS-like symptoms.Both are influenced by the gut microbiome and gut-immune interactions, an active area of ongoing research.Symptom flares in both can be triggered or worsened by stress, certain foods, and poor sleep.How a Root-Cause Approach Looks at IBS SymptomsEven though IBS isn't autoimmune, a functional medicine evaluation can still be useful for IBS-pattern symptoms — assessing gut microbiome balance, food sensitivities, prior infections, and stress-related gut-brain axis factors that often drive IBS symptoms, while ruling out or monitoring for autoimmune digestive conditions when the symptom picture warrants it.Ready for Personalized Answers?General information is a starting point — a Discovery Call helps us look at your specific labs, symptoms, and history to build a plan that's actually yours.Book your Discovery CallFrequently Asked Questions01Can IBS turn into an autoimmune disease over time?IBS itself is not currently understood to progress into an autoimmune disease.
